rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

examples: This non-opening story card has three sentences: the ground waiting, God not using gold or marble, and the teaser about the humbler material. Trim it to one or two sentences.
This story card has three sentences, including Papa Dorin's comment about the 25 cent bin. Condense it to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: “ANY tree?”, the parking comparison, and the woman's correction. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.

places.problem: This non-opening story card has three sentences: the ground waiting, God not using gold or marble, and the teaser about the humbler material. Trim it to one or two sentences.
This story card has three sentences, including Papa Dorin's comment about the 25 cent bin. Condense it to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: “ANY tree?”, the parking comparison, and the woman's correction. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Cain's statement, “Heavy words, friend.” and “Let them sit a second.”
This story card has four sentences. Summarizing the genealogy and trades in one card is appropriate, but the summary is still over the story-card sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: one about Shem, one about Peleg and Joktan, and one about Papa Dorin's cutters.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the scattering statement, 'Big plans, baker,' and 'Bigger God.' The closing quip needs to be combined into one sentence or otherwise shortened to keep the card within the two-sentence limit.
This genealogy summary is three sentences long. Since it is not the stop's opening card, it exceeds the two-sentence limit for story cards.
This non-opening story card is punctuated as three sentences: the preparation sentence, "Early, friend." and "The very next morning."
This story card is punctuated as three sentences: the settlement sentence, "Me?" and the mustache punchline.
The genealogy summary, the Rebekah detail and the story-continuation line make three sentences on a non-opening story card.
This non-opening story card has three sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has four sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: "And once more, son number four: Judah.", "FOUR, friend.", and "At this rate Leah's gonna need a bigger tent." Story cards after the opening card are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about the three-day journey, the burnt-cookie question, and the zip-code punchline. It needs to be shortened to one or two sentences.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the narrative sentence, 'A family meeting in a field full of sheep.' and 'Friend, that is a LOT of listeners.' It needs to be reduced to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the angel's quoted statement, 'In other words: Jacob, you KNOW Me.' and 'We've met.' It needs to be reduced to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the pursuit and arrival, "Seven days, friend!", and the joke about Papa Dorin's base. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card exceeds the sentence limit. "Four hundred men.", "FOUR.", and "HUNDRED." already create three sentence-like units before the final sentence about Jacob dividing the children.
This non-opening story card has four sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has four sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentence units: Joseph's reply, "Me?", and the alarm-and-snooze sentence.
This non-opening story card has three sentence units: the robe-stripping sentence, "THE robe.", and "The robe of many colors he's wearing."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the attribution accompanying "No," the Sheol quotation, and the sentence about Jacob weeping and Papa Dorin missing his kids.
This non-opening story card has three sentences or sentence fragments: the main sentence, "Well." and "Almost any of it." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the question “And the chief baker?”, the sentence about his being hanged, and the concluding sentence about both interpretations coming true.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence about collecting and storing the grain, the question ending in “and me?”, and the sentence about payday and the couch cushions.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence about the famine, the question about the man selling grain, and the sentence identifying Joseph.
This story card has three sentences: the opening question, the sentence about the missing brother, and the group-chat joke.

This story card exceeds the limit with three sentences of narration: the introduction to Jacob's quotation, "Friend, I know that feeling," and the sentence about the junk drawer. Jacob's quotation also contains two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Israel gives in, he instructs his sons about the gift, and Papa Dorin adds a joke. It needs to be condensed to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the vision, the dough joke, and Jacob's answer. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This summary has three sentences: the description of the list, "Seventy in all.", and the cookie-cutter joke. That exceeds the two-sentence limit for a non-opening story card.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the exclamation about Jacob's age, the junk-drawer reaction, and the setup for his burial request.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the embalming statement, the one-word sentence FORTY., and the oven joke.
This story card has three sentences: Joseph's return, Promise kept, friend., and the final CAME BACK sentence.

This story card has three sentences: “Pharaoh wants Moses dead.”, “So Moses does what anybody would do, friend.”, and “He RUNS.” Only the opening card may have up to three sentences; this card needs to be reduced to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the travel sentence, the question about the donkey, and the junk-drawer reaction.
This is not the walkthrough's opening card, but it has three sentences: the LORD's instruction, “That's the WHOLE address,” and the sentence about having no pin or landmark.
The card runs beyond the two-sentence limit with the gathering sentence, the meeting question, “Yeah.” and “THAT moment.”
This story card has three sentences: “SLACKERS!”, “Slackers!”, and the sentence beginning “And that's why”. Since this is not an opening card, it exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card exceeds the two-sentence limit. Even treating "FROGS. IN. THE. OVENS." as one emphatic outburst rather than four fragments, it is followed by two additional full sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "And not just a few.", the statement about all the dust turning into gnats, and the junk-drawer joke. Combine or trim them to two.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the question about asking for silver and gold, the coupon joke, and the teaser about the Egyptians' reaction.
This non-opening story card has three full sentences plus a question fragment, exceeding the limit of one or two sentences.

This non-opening story card has four sentences: the summary, the donkey and eye-for-eye details, the cookie-dough sentence, and 'I looked.' Condense it to no more than two sentences while retaining the long-stretch summary.
This non-opening story card has four sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences: “Altar's up.” “Pillars are up.” and the sentence about the offerings. It exceeds the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the goat-hair tent sentence, "That's my kind of instructions, friend," and the recipe sentence.
This story card has three sentences: "It's a land flowing with milk and honey," "Sounds perfect, right?" and "Then God says the next part...." Only the opening card may have three sentences.
This story card is punctuated as three sentences: the Israelites stripping off their jewelry, "Me?" and the sentence about flour in Papa Dorin's mustache. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the rule about the flesh and clay pot, the standalone exclamation "BROKEN!", and the junk-drawer joke.
This story card has three sentences: the third-day warning, the question ending in "but this meat?", and "Hands OFF."
This non-opening story card has three standalone sentences or utterances: 'Moses hears Aaron out...', 'Me?', and 'Somebody explains themselves...'. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card runs to four sentences: the statement about touching things, the question about carrying them, the command to wash and bathe, and the moving-crew punchline.

This non-opening story card runs to four short sentences or sentence fragments: the Scripture statement, "Complete rest.", "No oven, no timer, NOTHING." and the mustache line. It needs to be condensed to one or two sentences.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Then comes a long list," the summary of the prohibitions, and the sentence about the reasons God gives. It needs to be condensed to no more than two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about revenge and grudges, the question about the replacement stamper, and the quoted reply.
This non-opening story card runs beyond two sentences: the quotation itself contains two sentences, followed by the separate lines “No fine print, friend.” and “No 'terms may vary.'”
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about God calling the Israelites His servants twice, the sentence about Egypt and His closing words, and the continuation line.
This non-opening story card has three sentences or sentence fragments: the diseases and fever, "And those harvests that ran into each other?" and "Now they'll sow their seed in vain."
This non-opening story card has four sentences or sentence fragments: the opening statement about the bread, "TEN bakers.", "ONE oven.", and "Friend, let that sink in."
This story card has five sentences. Only the opening card may be longer than two sentences.
This story card has four sentences. Only the opening card may be longer than two sentences.
This non-opening story card runs three sentences: the narration followed by "A whole TRIBE, friend." and "Presented to ONE man."
This story card runs four sentences, including the two-sentence jealousy joke, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This story card runs three sentences: Moses' obedience, the reaction to the one-month age threshold, and the roster joke.
The long-stretch summary runs five sentences. Being a summary makes the stretch one beat, but it does not exempt the card from the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card runs four sentences, including the two short number statements and the two-sentence cookie-box joke.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence about counting the Gershonites, "The LORD is consistent, and me?" and the sentence about Papa Dorin's cookie batches. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
Non-opening story cards 3, 5, 6, 8, 12 and 15 each exceed two sentences. Card 3 runs to five short punctuated sentences and card 6 to four; the others run to three.
Story cards 1, 5 and 9 each exceed the two-sentence limit for non-opening story cards.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the introduction to line three, the standalone exclamation "Peace!", and the sentence about the batteries. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card has at least three sentences: the quarrel, "Friend, I know that voice," and the flat-batch joke. That exceeds the one-to-two-sentence limit even before counting the additional sentence inside Papa Dorin's quoted joke.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Moses' intercession, "That's a big heart, friend," and the group-chat joke. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the poets' quotation, the sentence about the drawer, and "Sihon's city gets a whole one."
Several non-opening story cards exceed two sentences: stop 1 cards 6 and 15, and stop 2 cards 1, 9, 11 and 13.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: “And not just any strength.” “Strength like a wild ox.” “Then Balaam turns to the subject of spells and divination.”
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the order to count, the pencil line, and "A BIG one." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card runs to four sentence-length units: "Count's done.", the inheritance sentence, "See?", and "The counting PAYS OFF." It needs to be compressed to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the LORD answering, the comment about God weighing in, and "Ohhh, baker, it is getting GOOD."
Several non-opening story cards exceed the two-sentence limit: stop 1 card 7 and stop 2 cards 1 and 2 each have three sentences, while stop 2 card 8 has four.
Several non-opening story cards run to three sentences when their short reaction lines are counted: stop 1 cards 3, 8 and 12; stop 2 card 9; and stop 3 cards 6, 11 and 15.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about crossing the Jordan, the question about paying guests and the line addressed to Sihon. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card has four punctuated sentence units: the statement about God giving the cities, the statement about the walls, "Me?" and the takeout-menu sentence. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has five sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has four sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has four sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has six sentences. It is not the walkthrough's opening card, so it exceeds the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about Egypt, 'Iron furnace, friend.' and the oven punchline. It needs to be tightened to one or two sentences.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about the man-made gods, the question about smelling a fresh batch and the cookie-stamper punchline. It needs to be tightened to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the list of locations, "Every green tree, friend!", and the dust-drawer joke. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sacrifice's source, Moses being particular about the location, and "Not 'eh, wherever.'" That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences: the arrival of the Feast of Weeks, the seven weeks of counting, and the junk-drawer joke. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Moses and the priests speaking, the nation-sized crowd, and the mixer joke.
This story card has three period-ended sentences: the curse, the restatement about taking money, and Papa Dorin's reaction.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: 'Nope.', the statement about lending and borrowing, and the payment-email joke. Story cards other than the opening card are limited to two sentences.

This non-opening story card exceeds two sentences: the opening statement about the stars, the sentence about losing count of the sprinkles, and then 'The stars?' and 'Forget it.' The joke can remain while being compressed into the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentence units: the crowd description, the setup ending with "and honestly?" and "He left EARLY." Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: 'And not halfway, either.', 'With all their heart and all their soul, Moses says.', and 'Then it's God's move.' That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This story card has four sentence units, including 'Not them.' and 'The LORD.', rather than the permitted one or two sentences.
This story card has three sentence units: the opening question, 'They don't just vanish.', and 'They get a NEW ADDRESS.' It needs to fit within two sentences.
This story card has four sentences: the statement about the land, the oven-timer setup, and separate sentences about listening and ignoring the timer. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: one about proclaiming the LORD's name, one about the solid name, and one beginning "Doesn't move, doesn't crack."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the retelling of verse 7, "Friend, nobody has to ask ME twice.", and the sentence about junk drawer stories.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence about wandering, "Forty YEARS.", and the junk-drawer joke.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the LORD's statement, the PAST DUE question, and "Like THAT, times a thousand."
This non-opening story card is five sentences long: the quoted sentence followed by four more sentences. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the verse 27 update, the apron instruction, and the sentence saying that more of the story is coming. It needs to be compressed to two sentences while retaining the required continuation line.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the introduction of Sihon and Og, the price-sticker joke, and the statement about Moses and the Israelites striking them down.
This non-opening summary story card has three sentences: the description of the western land, the roll call of kings, and the joke about the total.
This non-opening story card runs to four sentences, including "Yes, friend." and "THAT Jerusalem."
The closing story card has four sentences rather than the permitted one or two.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "But hold on.", "Hold on, hold on, HOLD ON.", and the following "What if..." question. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This long-stretch summary runs for four dense sentences, although a non-opening story card is limited to 1 to 2 sentences. It needs to be condensed while remaining one summary card for the stretch.
This story card has four sentences: the two 'Hold on' sentences, the sentence about Israel's trouble, and the sentence about the LORD raising up judges.
The opening sentence, the statement about the LORD raising a judge with 'EVERY. SINGLE. TIME.' broken into separate pieces, and the closing rescue sentence run past the two-sentence limit.
'Now it gets quiet, friend.' and 'Real quiet.' are followed by the longer sentence about the LORD's anger and speech, making three sentences.
'Ohhh.' plus the two sentences that follow gives this story card three sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the numbers leaving and remaining, "I've seen that move, friend," and the boss-and-parking-lot sentence.
Story cards 1, 7 and 9 each contain three sentences. None is the walkthrough's opening card, so each is limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the fact about Gideon's sons, Papa Dorin's joke, and the setup about Abimelech's question.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Big talk.", the group-chat comparison, and the sentence about Zebul hearing Gaal and burning with anger.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Round one is over.", the sentence about Abimelech and Zebul, and the joke about Gaal not unpacking.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Jephthah's in charge now.", "His first move?", and "He sends messengers to the king of the Ammonites."
This story card has three sentences: the account of Israel's detour, "A WHOLE nation on a detour.", and the GPS punchline. It is not the opening card, so it is limited to two sentences.

The final story card has three sentences: the summary of the king's response, "Keep that oven warm, baker.", and "We are NOT done with Jephthah yet." The story-isn't-over line does not create an exception to the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences. Trim or combine the storyteller line and joke so the card stays within two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the capture of the fords, the line about crossing the river, and the airport-security joke.
This non-opening story card runs to four sentences, including "SEVENTY." The summary and its joke need to fit within two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the angel's arrival, "Not to Manoah." and "To his wife." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the razor statement, "No razor, friend." and the mustache reaction. It needs to be compressed to one or two sentences.
This story card has three sentences. Only the walkthrough's opening card may be that long; this is the opening of the second stop, not the opening card of the walkthrough.

This story card is written as four standalone sentences or sentence fragments: the bowstrings, the ropes, the scam-call comparison, and Delilah's renewed question. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
The emphatic 'Every day. EVERY. DAY.' followed by the closing sentence gives this story card four standalone sentences or fragments, exceeding the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card exceeds two sentences: after the sentences about returning the silver and the curse and blessing, it adds a separate question fragment and the standalone punchline 'SAME GUY.'

This non-opening story card has three sentences: "They stay there four months.", "Four MONTHS on a rock.", and the sentence about Papa Dorin's years in the junk drawer. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Boaz's greeting, the workplace joke, and the harvesters' reply.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the fork action, "This man is NOT picky, friend," and "If it's boiling, he's in it." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Five more children," "FIVE," and the sentence about Samuel growing up. It needs to fit within two sentences.
This non-opening story card exceeds the two-sentence limit: "The GROUND." and "SHAKES." are separate sentence units, followed by the sentence about Mags and the Philistines.
This non-opening story card has three sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has four sentences: the two quoted sentences and the two snooze-button sentences. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
Even without counting the fragment 'But WHO?', this non-opening story card has four sentences. The story-continuation line does not exempt it from the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Samuel's "Stop!", his statement about telling Saul what the LORD said, and Saul's reply.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Samuel's question, the rhetorical question about replacing Saul, and the workplace comparison. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the peace reply, the statement about coming to sacrifice, and the instruction to consecrate themselves. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences: Jesse's report about his youngest son, the question about being stuck out back, and Papa Dorin's drawer reaction. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences: the youngest son's arrival and description, the interjection calling for a pause, and the callback about Eliab. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Saul's command, "And one of the servants?" and "He already knows a guy."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the message to Jesse, the comment about David being out in a field, and the CEO comparison.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the move to Bethlehem, Jesse's family, and the three oldest brothers following Saul. Story cards after the opening are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card is broken into three sentences: the stone sinking and Goliath falling, "Six cubits and a span, flat on his face.", and "ONE stone." It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has four sentence-length units: the opening statement, "Saul.", "LISTENS.", and Papa Dorin's closing reaction. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences once Saul's two-sentence quotation is included: the idol setup, Saul's question, and his accusation.
This non-opening story card has three sentence-length units: its opening summary, the question fragment about Saul and David, and "It's nowhere near done."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Jonathan's answer, the assurance that he would tell David, and David's follow-up question.
The seating sentence, "And David's seat?" and "EMPTY, and nothing at a dinner table talks louder than an empty chair" make three sentence units on a non-opening story card.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the report about David's followers, "Friend, that's not an army," and the DMV punchline.
This non-opening story card exceeds two sentences. Gad's quotation contains two sentences, followed by a separate sentence about David leaving and another sentence for the snooze-button joke.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Saul's complaint, "Not ONE," and the group-chat joke.
This story card exceeds two sentences: the résumé sentence is followed by Ahimelech's quoted question and the separate exclamation, "Far be it from me!"
This final story card has three sentences: the two sentences quoted from David and the additional story-continuation sentence.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence about Achish trusting David, the sentence about the Philistines gathering for war, and the standalone "Uh-oh." Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
Several non-opening story cards exceed two sentences: stop 1 cards 7 and 9 each have four, stop 1 card 11 has three when Saul's two quoted sentences are counted, and stop 2 card 19 has three.
This non-opening story card has three sentences.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: "They journey all night to get them.", "All night, friend.", and "I can't make it past the second oven timer without nodding off." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the narration about the messengers, "No text, no group chat, friend.", and the final joke. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card runs well past two sentences. Joab's quotation contains several sentences, and Papa Dorin adds two more sentences after it.
This is not the passage's opening card, but it uses three sentences: one about Abner's death, one about David's orders, and one joke about Joab's assignment.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the Jebusites' thought, the chocolate-chip-bin comparison, and "Famous last words." It exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This story card runs for more than two sentences, including the separate exclamation "ELEVEN!" and the closing bakery joke. The long-stretch summary rule does not exempt it from the story-card sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the Hadadezer sentence, the cooling-rack setup, and “The cooling rack won.”
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Joab's quotation, "Fight hard, then leave it with the LORD," and "That's the whole plan."

This non-opening story card has three sentences: Ziba's response, the comment about the donkeys and Mephibosheth's property, and the workplace comparison. Non-opening story cards are limited to two sentences.
This non-opening story card has four sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This is not an opening card, but it has three sentences: the introduction to the list, the sentence about Uriah, and "Thirty-seven in all."
Several non-opening story cards exceed the sentence limit: card 4 has four sentences, card 9 has three, card 10 has four, and card 12 has three.
This non-opening story card has three sentences when "Me?" is counted, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This story card is punctuated as five sentences, including "Me?" and "Twenty-five cents.", well beyond the two-sentence limit for a non-opening story card.
This non-opening story card runs for six sentences, including the Gezer explanation and the two-sentence wedding-gift joke. It needs to be condensed to the bite-sized limit.

This story card has four sentences, counting the closing joke. It also stacks the yearly revenue, shields, cups, ship cargo, throne and lions in one dense card rather than keeping the summary to the two-sentence limit.
This story card has four sentences: the tribute, the chariots and silver, the import and export trade, and the parking joke. That exceeds the limit for a non-opening story card.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence listing the women and nations, followed by two separate joke sentences. It needs to be trimmed or combined into no more than two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: two inside Ahijah's quoted greeting and then Papa Dorin's joke about the disguise.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Then Elijah picks up stones." "Twelve of them, friend." "Not eleven, not thirteen." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the instruction from Jezebel's letter, the question about the seat of honor, and "I don't trust it."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Naboth is gone.", the report sent to Jezebel, and "And Jezebel goes to her husband."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the introduction of Jehoshaphat and the king of Israel, "Two kingdoms, side by side." and "So how do these two get along?"
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Wrecked at Ezion-geber.", "Never even left." and the sentence carrying Papa Dorin's dough-tray comparison.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the recap of the death message, the line about Ahaziah's next question, and the question about the man's appearance.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Ahaziah not needing another clue, his identification of Elijah, and the business-card joke.
This non-opening story card runs to three sentences or sentence fragments: the narrative setup, 'Fifty men.', and 'For one hairy guy who is SITTING DOWN.'

This non-opening story card has three sentences: Elisha's initial reply, "Do not speak of it," and the separate sentence introducing Elijah's next request. Non-opening story cards are limited to two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the narration about the prophets at Jericho, the oven-timer comparison ending in "I KNOW," and the final standalone "I KNOW."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Jehoshaphat's pledge, 'THAT is a friend,' and the question about which route to take. The limit is two sentences.

The retrieval, the drawer comparison and the extended jealousy punchline run well beyond two sentences. Even without counting the emphatic "IRON. FLOATING." fragments, the card exceeds the story-card sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the reaction "Yep.", the statement that Jeroboam does evil, and the sentence about restoring Israel's borders.
This story card has three sentences: "Back up north.", the sentence introducing Zechariah's reign, and "Friend, don't get too attached to this one." It is not the walkthrough's opening card.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Six months.", the sentence about Zechariah's evil, and the sentence introducing Shallum's conspiracy.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the summary of the list, 'And the Sepharvites go further,' and the sentence about their child sacrifice. It needs to be no more than two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the quoted verse, "One night." and "That's all it took, friend."
This story card has three sentence units: "That's the message.", "Straight, no sprinkles.", and "So Hezekiah turns his face to the wall." A non-opening story card is limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card uses three separate sentences or sentence fragments: "The king stops." "Looks." "And asks, 'What is this monument I see?'"
Five non-opening story cards exceed the two-sentence limit: card 4 has five sentences, card 5 has three, card 8 has three, card 10 has four and card 12 has five.
This non-opening story card runs for four sentences, including the Elkanah joke and the detail about Samuel's sons. It exceeds the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card introduces all three singers, summarizes their positions and then tells a multi-sentence oven joke. It runs well beyond the two sentences allowed for a non-opening story card.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

examples: The earlier cards have said only that their eyes were opened. They have not mentioned nakedness or a need for coverings, so the baker cannot reason out “naked”; the blank tests unseen wording.

The setup quotes the general curse but gives no context from which the serpent's new movement can be inferred. “Belly” is therefore an unseen word the baker must guess rather than a meaning supported by the earlier cards.
Card 1 says only that Adam gives his wife a name. Nothing in the earlier cards allows the baker to reason out “Eve,” so this blank simply asks for an unseen name.

The earlier cards do not identify Babylon or provide enough context to infer it. The baker must guess an unseen word from the line rather than reason out its meaning.

The setup gives the baker no basis for inferring the unseen image of drunkenness. The blank therefore asks for wording the baker has not seen rather than a meaning they can reason out.

Nothing in the earlier cards points to Judah or Jerusalem. The baker must guess two place names from the unread verse rather than reason out their meaning from the setup.

The earlier cards give no way to reason out that the Spirit descends like a dove rather than a flame or a cloud. This blank asks the baker to guess an unseen word from the verse instead of testing its meaning.

Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason out “twelve.” The blank asks for an unseen number, so the baker must rely on luck or prior knowledge rather than reasoning from the walkthrough.
The earlier cards give no basis for choosing “flute” over “harp” or “trumpet.” This blank tests an unseen detail rather than meaning the baker can reason out.

The card makes the baker complete the woman's not-yet-presented reply by supplying the BSB word "crumbs." The blank is a near-verbatim continuation of verse 27, so it asks for the next wording of her line rather than testing a paraphrased meaning.

The blank asks for a detail the earlier cards give no clue about. A baker cannot reason out whether Jesus specifies the first, biggest or last fish, so this is a lucky guess at unseen wording rather than a test of meaning.

The setup gives the baker no basis to choose a camel rather than a donkey or an ox. All three animals fit the impossible picture, so the blank tests the unseen wording of Jesus' line instead of a meaning the baker can reason out.

No earlier card identifies the tax coin or gives a clue that distinguishes a denarius from a shekel or drachma. A baker using only the earlier cards can choose "denarius" only through prior knowledge or luck, so this blank tests wording they have not seen rather than meaning they can reason out.
Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason out "angels" rather than "stars" or "elders." The blank asks for wording from a line the baker has not yet seen.

The setup only says that the people will be separated as sheep and goats. Nothing earlier lets the baker reason out their placement, so the blanks simply ask for the unseen wording of verse 33: right and left.

Nothing in the earlier cards gives the baker a basis for choosing whether the angel sits, stands or kneels on the stone. All three actions are equally plausible, so the blank quizzes an unseen verb rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.

Neither blank can be reasoned out from the earlier cards, which have not introduced the priest, Moses or the cleansing instructions. The blanks ask for wording and details the baker has not seen rather than meaning supported by the setup.
The earlier cards give no basis for reasoning that 'sinners,' rather than 'soldiers' or 'priests,' belongs in the blank. The baker can only guess wording from a verse they have not yet seen.
The preceding card gives no basis for choosing "word" over "law" or "promise." The blank asks for wording the baker has not seen rather than a meaning they can reason out from the earlier cards.
Jesus's question about comparing the kingdom gives no clue that the answer is mustard, and mustard, cumin and barley are all plausible seeds. The baker can only guess the unseen wording.

The blank asks for 'hands' from wording the baker has not seen, and the earlier cards do not give enough context to reason it out rather than 'cloak' or 'staff'. It tests an unheard word instead of an inferable meaning.

Nothing on the earlier cards indicates how the hearers respond to Jesus' teaching. Astonished, unmoved and silent are all compatible with that setup, so the blank asks for an unseen reaction rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.

No earlier card names or hints at Jesus' mother. Knowing that the crowd mentions His trade and family does not let the baker reason out Mary rather than Elizabeth or Martha, so this blank depends on prior knowledge or luck.

The preceding cards do not establish Jesus' emotional response to the unbelief. Amazed, angry and grieved are all plausible reactions to the setup, so the baker cannot reason out the blank from what has been shown.

The blank asks for "market," an unseen detail that cannot be reasoned out from the earlier cards. Temple and fields are also plausible places to return from, so the baker must guess rather than demonstrate understanding.
Nothing in the earlier cards gives the baker a basis for choosing “mute” over “blind” or “lame.” The blank asks for an unseen detail that can only be guessed.

The blank asks for "Gentiles," but the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out that group rather than the Levites or Pharisees. The baker can only guess wording that has not yet been introduced.
Nothing in the earlier cards connects David to the coming kingdom, so filling in his name means guessing wording the baker has not seen rather than reasoning out the passage's meaning.

The opening card does not establish that the planned trap is verbal, so the baker cannot reason out 'words' rather than 'deeds' or 'plans.' The blank asks for unseen BSB wording instead of testing a meaning supported by the earlier card.
The earlier cards establish that risen people will not marry, but they provide no basis for reasoning that Jesus compares them to angels. The baker must guess the unseen next word of His line.

Nothing before this card identifies whom the second commandment says to love. Completing Jesus' line with 'neighbor' is therefore a guess at wording the baker has not seen, rather than a reasoned answer from the setup.

The blank asks the baker to recover an unseen object from the verse. This tests wording rather than a meaning the baker can infer.

The setup says only that the Son of Man sends out angels; it gives no clue about their task. Choosing gather rather than judge or warn therefore depends on knowing the unseen BSB wording, not on reasoning out the meaning.

The earlier cards give no basis for distinguishing 'grieved' from 'angry' or 'afraid'. The blank therefore asks the baker to guess the previously unseen wording of the disciples' reaction rather than reason out its meaning.
The setup says only that Jesus blessed, broke and gave the disciples bread. It provides no basis for inferring 'body' rather than 'word' or 'gift', so the baker must guess Jesus' unseen wording.
Calling Jesus' next statement a promise after hard news does not enable the baker to infer either 'risen' or 'Galilee'. Both blanks require guessing details that the earlier cards have not supplied.

The setup only says that the centurion saw how Jesus died and then spoke. It gives no basis for reasoning out “Son” rather than “Servant” or “Prophet,” so the baker can only guess the unseen wording of the centurion's line.

Nothing in the earlier cards gives the baker a way to reason out the name John. Samuel and Isaac are equally plausible without already knowing Luke 1:13, so this blank tests unseen wording rather than an inferable meaning.

The blank asks the baker to complete the unseen wording of Gabriel's statement with “Holy.” “Chosen” and “Anointed” are also plausible Bible-sounding titles, so the card tests wording rather than a meaning the baker can reasonably work out.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

examples: The phrase "that tree" points back to choice card 15, which the baker can no longer see. Make the question self-contained by identifying the forbidden tree.
“All of that” points back to the three descriptions on story card 9, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to supply the relevant context itself.
“After this” depends on the preceding story card, which is no longer visible. The question does not identify the statement or event that “this” refers to, so it is not self-contained.

places.problem: The phrase "that tree" points back to choice card 15, which the baker can no longer see. Make the question self-contained by identifying the forbidden tree.

“After this” depends on the preceding story card, which is no longer visible. The question does not identify the statement or event that “this” refers to, so it is not self-contained.

“That plain” points back to earlier cards instead of identifying the plain within the question itself. The question should supply the context, such as naming the plain of the Jordan.

"This time" and "the same thing" do not identify the Nile being turned to blood. The question depends on context from cards that are no longer on screen instead of saying what the magicians are supposedly unable to repeat.

"Write it on a scroll" again leaves the pronoun's antecedent on an earlier card. The question should say what Moses is recording rather than relying on context the baker cannot see.

"They" has no antecedent within the question. The question itself needs to identify the Israelites as the people serving God.
"Them" has no antecedent within the question. It should name the Israelites rather than relying on the preceding cards to identify who will have sickness taken away.

The question points back to card 12 with "that oil" and does not identify the pure olive oil for the tabernacle light within the question itself.
