Cards 8-10 give only his knowledge and the result that no offspring was produced, then refer to "what Onan did" without explaining the deed. This omits a central detail and leaves verse 10 less clear.

Joseph's actual reaction in Genesis 50:17, weeping when the message arrives, is never told. Marking anger as false only says what he did not do and leaves an important detail of the reconciliation uncovered.

Pharaoh's fear in Exodus 1:10 also includes the possibility that the Israelites will leave the country, but no card covers that detail. It is an important part of his stated concern and helps explain why he oppresses them rather than simply wanting them gone.

The walkthrough never states what actually happens to an unredeemed firstborn donkey. Exodus 13:13 says its neck is to be broken, but marking this statement false only rules out keeping it for work and leaves that part of the instruction untold.

Exodus 13:22 says that neither the pillar of cloud nor the pillar of fire left its place, but the walkthrough addresses only the cloud. No other card supplies the fire's constancy, and the final story card contains only the closing line.

The correct answer omits God's command to ordain Aaron and his sons. Exodus 28:41 calls for Moses to anoint, ordain, and consecrate them, and no other card covers ordination, so an important step in their preparation for priestly service is missing.

The card says that the LORD will do what Moses asked but omits His stated reason in verse 17: Moses has found favor in His sight, and He knows Moses by name. God's own confirmation of those things explains His answer and completes Moses's appeal from verses 12-13, so this is an important detail to leave out.

The walkthrough never tells the baker that the unchanged article in verse 55 must be burned. Marking the statement False only establishes that the item is not clean; cards 5 and 9 cover burning after mildew spreads or reappears, leaving this distinct outcome untold.

This false statement only establishes that the uncleanness does not last seven days. No card ever supplies Leviticus 14:46's actual detail that anyone entering the closed house is unclean until evening, leaving that important duration untaught.

Only the first part of Leviticus 20:5 is covered. The walkthrough never says that the LORD will also cut off from among their people both the man and all who follow him in prostituting themselves with Molech, leaving out an important part of the judgment.

Only the first sentence of Leviticus 20:25 is covered. The command not to become contaminated by any animal, bird or crawling thing, together with the LORD's statement that He set these apart as unclean, is never told.

Leviticus 22:11 permits both a slave bought with the priest's own money and a slave born in his household to eat his food. The walkthrough teaches only the household-born slave, leaving the purchased-slave exception entirely covered nowhere.

The answer reduces Leviticus 22:19 to “an unblemished male animal,” and no other card explains that it must be from the cattle, sheep, or goats. A baker could leave thinking any unblemished male animal qualifies.

The stop gives the penalty of being cut off but never covers the rest of Numbers 9:13: this happens because the man did not present the LORD's offering at its appointed time, and he will bear the consequences of his sin. Those stated reasons and consequences are important to understanding the verse.
No card covers the statement in Numbers 12:8 that Moses sees the form of the LORD. This is a distinct and important part of God's explanation of how Moses differs from other prophets.
Numbers 21:6 says that many Israelites were bitten and died. This card only addresses whether a few were bitten, and no other card mentions the deaths, leaving out an important detail of the passage.

The card only establishes that Israel did not make peace with the Amorites at Jazer. Neither this card nor any later card says that Israel captured its villages and drove out the Amorites, so the actual event in Numbers 21:32 is left untaught.

The coverage of Numbers 23:24 stops at naming the lioness and the lion. The cards never tell that the people do not rest until they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain, leaving out the close of Balaam's second oracle.

Marking "they get no land at all" false explains only what does not happen. No card tells the actual outcome in Numbers 32:30: if they do not cross armed, they must accept their possession among the other Israelites in Canaan. This leaves a key part of Moses' agreement untaught.

Deuteronomy 2:11 is skipped entirely. The baker is never told that the Emites, like the Anakites, were regarded as Rephaim. Besides losing that part of Moses' historical note, this leaves 'land of the Rephaim too' in card 17 without the earlier description that 'too' points back to.

Deuteronomy 16:12 also commands Israel to carefully follow these statutes, but no card covers that command. The only card addressing verse 12 asks solely about remembering their slavery in Egypt, leaving an important part of the passage untaught.

The correct answer establishes only that the tribes on Mount Ebal are not there to bless the people. No card explicitly supplies verse 13's important positive detail that they are there to deliver the curse.

This is the only card covering Joshua 4:23, and answering False establishes only that the comparison was not to the Sea of Galilee. No card ever tells the baker that the LORD had dried up the Red Sea, leaving out an important detail of the passage.

This false statement is the walkthrough's only coverage of verse 13. Its negation says merely that Israel did not burn all the other cities built on their mounds; it does not teach that Israel burned none of them and that Hazor was the only exception. No later card supplies that detail.

The walkthrough never says that the ephod became a snare to Gideon and his household. Marking the blessing statement false establishes only that it was not a blessing, leaving this central consequence of Judges 8:27 untaught before the cards move on.

The walkthrough never tells what the Danites actually say in Judges 18:25. This card only rules out an offer of repayment, and card 13 says merely that they warn Micah not to raise his voice. The explicit threat that angry men will attack Micah and that he and his family will lose their lives is omitted, leaving out a key detail of the confrontation.

The actual endpoint in Ruth 2:23 is never stated. Card 17 only establishes that staying only until the barley harvest is false, and this card's 'all that time' does not explain that Ruth gleans until both the barley and wheat harvests are finished.

The retelling of verse 7 omits Saul's claim that God has delivered David into his hand, and no later card supplies it. This is an important part of Saul's response and contrasts with verse 14, where God would not deliver David into Saul's hand.

Verse 10's report that Saul intends to destroy Keilah on David's account is omitted here and never covered later. David's concern for the city is an important part of his prayer and of the danger facing Keilah.

The walkthrough never clearly establishes that the woman served the food and that Saul and his servants ate. Card 18 places their eating inside a compound statement marked False, and this card clarifies only that they left. A baker could therefore miss, or even negate, the eating in verse 25.

The walkthrough never says that Josheb-basshebeth killed the eight hundred men. "Take on" only says that he fought them, and the follow-up on card 3 does not supply the outcome either, leaving out the key result of his exploit in verse 8.

The walkthrough never communicates a key part of the queen's praise in 1 Kings 10:9: the LORD delighted in Solomon and made him king because of His eternal love for Israel. Cards 13 and 14 cover only whom she blesses and Solomon's task, leaving out this important reason.

Jehu's repeated command, "Fall in behind me," is never told in either verse 18 or verse 19. Card 8 only establishes that the first rider was not sent back, so the baker never learns that both messengers fell in behind Jehu, the repeated action behind the watchman's reports.

Although cards 15-17 cover verses 35-37, the walkthrough never states the verse 36 prophecy that dogs would devour Jezebel's flesh. This skips the central explanation for the few remains they find and a key part of the prophecy's fulfillment.

Verse 11 is reduced to the request being in Solomon's heart. The walkthrough never conveys its central contrast: Solomon did not request riches, wealth, honor, his enemies' death, or even long life, but wisdom and knowledge to govern God's people. This leaves out God's stated reason for His response in verses 11-12.

This is the only card on 2 Chronicles 6:41, but it covers only the call to arise with the ark. No card tells Solomon's petitions that the priests be clothed with salvation and that the godly ones rejoice in goodness, leaving an important part of the closing prayer uncovered.

The central action of verse 4 is never told: Jehoshaphat turned the people back to the LORD, the God of their fathers. The correct False answer only establishes that he did not gather soldiers, and no later card supplies what he actually did.

The correct answer only establishes that Ahaziah was not hiding in Jerusalem. Neither this card nor any later card gives the actual detail from 2 Chronicles 22:9 that he was hiding in Samaria, so the walkthrough never tells that part of his capture.

Verse 3 gives two reasons the Passover could not be kept at the regular time: too few priests had consecrated themselves, and the people had not gathered in Jerusalem. The correct option names only the first reason, and no other card tells the second, leaving the explanation of the delay incomplete.

Marking the statement False establishes only that the people did not release the conspirators. No card tells what verse 25 actually says happened: the people of the land killed all those who had conspired against Amon. The walkthrough then moves directly to Josiah, leaving out that event.

Marking the statement false establishes only that mourning was not limited to Josiah's servants. No card supplies the actual detail from verse 24 that all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him, leaving an important beat of the passage untold.

The walkthrough never includes the enemies' stated plan to kill the builders in Nehemiah 4:11. Cards 3-5 cover only sneaking in and ending the work, leaving out an important detail behind the armed defenses that follow.

The summary's only coverage of Nehemiah 7:61-65 is that some people could not prove their ancestry. It never tells that the priests who could not find their family records were excluded from the priesthood as unclean, or that they were barred from eating the most holy things until a priest could consult the Urim and Thummim. This leaves out the register's key consequential episode.

Esther 9:30 is covered only by denying that the letters contain warning and threat. Even when the baker correctly selects False, neither this card nor any later card supplies the actual detail that Mordecai sent words of peace and truth.

The walkthrough jumps from Job 30:21-23 on card 13 to Job 30:25 here, leaving Job 30:24 entirely untold. That verse is a distinct step in Job's complaint: no one stretches out his hand against a ruined man when he cries for help. Omitting it loses part of the flow into Job's appeal to his own compassion.

Answering False only establishes that Job's skin is not starting to heal. Neither this card nor any other tells what Job 30:30 actually says: his skin grows black and peels, and his bones burn with fever. The closing picture of his physical affliction is therefore not actually taught.

No card covers the warning in Psalm 2:12 that His wrath ignites in an instant. The stop mentions anger and perishing in rebellion but leaves out the suddenness of His wrath, an important detail in the closing warning.

The treatment of verse 13 in cards 16 and 17 never covers David's request that willful sins not rule over him. Card 16 establishes only that he mentions willful sins, and card 17 moves from God keeping him from them to the resulting blamelessness and cleansing. The request that sins not rule over him is an important part of the psalm's closing prayer.

The walkthrough never tells the first petition of Psalm 20:9: the direct request for the LORD to save the king. Card 15 only establishes that the person is the king, and this card covers only the request to answer us, leaving the closing petition incomplete.

Negating the invented statement about ruling far away does not actually tell the baker the positive petition in verse 7. No card states that the king is asked to sit enthroned in God's presence forever; in particular, the verse's "forever" is left uncovered.

The second half of verse 3 is handled only by negating the statement that Israel alone has seen God's salvation. No card supplies the positive detail that all the ends of the earth have seen it, leaving an important part of the verse's worldwide scope unstated.

Psalm 105:28 is used only for darkness, and the next card moves immediately to the waters becoming blood. The verse's closing movement, yet they defied His words, is never told or asked anywhere, leaving out an important response in the song.

A correct answer only establishes that the writer does not fear the rulers. Neither this card nor a later card supplies the verse's central positive contrast: his heart fears only God's word. That part of verse 161 is left untold.

Marking the statement False only establishes that the thrones are not the thrones of the house of Saul. No card ever supplies the actual detail from verse 5, that they are the thrones of the house of David, so an important part of the passage is left untold.

The setup says the prayer starts with who should prosper, but this false statement only rules out those who rule Jerusalem. No card ever reveals that David prays for those who love Jerusalem to prosper, leaving the baker without that detail from verse 6.

The positive detail in Psalm 130:5 that the writer puts his hope in the LORD's word is never taught. Card 7 stops the quotation before that detail, and marking this statement false only establishes that his hope is not in his own plans. An important part of the verse is left uncovered.
This false statement only rules out fear as the reason the people listen. Neither this card nor any later card supplies the reason verse 6 actually gives: David's words are pleasant.

The false statement merely negates seeking refuge in David's own strength. The walkthrough never positively recounts that David seeks refuge in God, and it omits his plea for God not to leave his soul defenseless.

The walkthrough covers the oxen, the unbroken walls and the absence of captivity from verse 14, but no card covers the remaining detail that there will be no cry of lament in the streets. This leaves David's closing picture of blessing incomplete.

The main outcome of Proverbs 16:7 is never told. The setup gives only the condition, and marking the statement about enemies running away as false does not teach that the LORD makes even the man's enemies live at peace with him.
The actual picture in Proverbs 16:26 is never told. Denying that hunger makes a worker give up does not teach that a worker's appetite works for him and that his hunger drives him onward.

Verse 15 appears only as a false statement that reverses both halves of the proverb. Answering False does not establish the actual contrast: gold and rubies are abundant, while lips of knowledge are the rare treasure. The baker is never clearly told what the verse does say.

The cards for verse 18 cover setting plans by consultation and mention war, but never teach its second instruction: wage war under sound guidance. Mentioning plans for war is not the same as telling the baker how Solomon says to wage it.

The walkthrough covers only the first half of verse 30, that lashes and wounds scour evil. No card tells the baker that beatings cleanse the inmost parts, leaving the verse's closing statement about inward cleansing untaught.
Only the image of a vanishing mist is taught from verse 6. No card mentions that making a fortune by a lying tongue is also a deadly pursuit, so the verse's warning about its deadly outcome is lost.

The setup only says that two groups react differently, and marking this statement False merely denies joy to the workers of iniquity. The walkthrough never actually teaches verse 15's contrast: justice executed is a joy to the righteous and a terror to the workers of iniquity.
The right answer gives only life and honor, omitting righteousness. Verse 21 says that the pursuer finds life, righteousness and honor, and no other card supplies the omitted result.

Answering False only establishes that the upright man does not harden his face too. Neither this card nor a story card tells the actual second half of verse 29, that the upright man makes his way sure.
The walkthrough covers only the command not to withhold discipline from Proverbs 23:13. It never tells the verse's other important detail: although the child is struck with a rod, he will not die.

The only card about Proverbs 27:13 covers taking the garment of the man who posts security for a stranger, but no card mentions the verse's second instruction: "get collateral if it is for a foreigner." That entire case is left out of the walkthrough.

This is the only card covering verse 27, but answering False never tells the baker what the locusts actually do. The verse's central detail is that they have no king, yet they all advance in formation; merely rejecting the claim that they scatter does not teach that detail.

This false statement about gold rafters is the walkthrough's only treatment of Song of Solomon 1:17. Even when the baker answers False, no card tells them what the verse actually says: the beams are cedars and the rafters are fragrant firs. The verse's actual picture is therefore left out.

The walkthrough repeatedly leaves out the passage's breast imagery, including every comparison in Song of Solomon 7:3, 7:7 and 7:8. Most importantly, cards 7-9 never explain that the palm tree's clusters of fruit picture her breasts, so card 8's climbing-and-fruit picture is not fully explained.

Verse 6's actual assignment is never told: taking spoils, seizing plunder and trampling the people like clay in the streets. Card 4 only rules out protecting the nation, and card 5 then refers back to "That's the job," leaving a central part of God's purpose for Assyria unexplained.

The card reduces Isaiah 13:16 to 'families suffer terribly,' never telling the baker that infants are dashed to pieces before their eyes and wives are ravished. It also drops the stabbing from verse 15. These omissions leave out the substance of the cited verses, not merely incidental detail.

Cards 6 and 7 never convey what happens to the eyes in Isaiah 32:3. They introduce the eyes but ask only about the ears, leaving out the detail that the eyes of those who see will no longer be closed.

Although this card cites Isaiah 35:8-9, it omits the important statement at the end of verse 9 that the redeemed will walk on the highway. No later card supplies that detail: card 19 says the redeemed return and enter Zion, but never connects them to walking on the Way.

Cards 8-9 cover the skies pouring down righteousness and imply that the earth opens, but never say that salvation may sprout and righteousness spring up with it, or that the LORD has created it. This leaves out the central result of Isaiah 45:8.

The only treatment of who sees God's salvation is a false statement saying it will be seen by Zion alone. Marking that false establishes only that the scope is wider than Zion; neither this card nor card 9 tells the central facts that the LORD bares His arm in the sight of all nations and that all the ends of the earth will see His salvation (Isaiah 52:10).

The stop ends without ever mentioning the LORD's promise in Isaiah 54:10 that His covenant of peace will not be broken. Card 19 covers His loving devotion, but the unbroken covenant of peace is another central promise in that verse.
Isaiah 56:5 promises the eunuchs both a memorial and a name, but no card mentions the memorial. Asking only about the name leaves out a central part of the promise.

The only treatment of the second half of verse 11 is the false statement that the Savior comes empty-handed. No card tells the baker that His reward is with Him and His recompense goes before Him, leaving an important part of the proclamation untaught.

The closing question elicits only "Sought Out," and no card mentions the verse's other name, "A City Not Forsaken." The walkthrough ends without teaching the full closing promise and its bookend to Zion's old name.

The only treatment of the last part of verse 20 is a false statement saying the person will be considered blessed. Marking it false establishes only that the person is not blessed; no card ever tells the baker that the verse says such a person will be considered accursed.

Verse 10 is reduced to an unnamed job list. Neither this card nor card 17 supplies the list, so the baker misses uprooting, tearing down, destroying and overthrowing, followed by building and planting. The true-or-false question only establishes that the work is not exclusively destructive.

No card mentions that the people also poured out drink offerings to other gods on these rooftops. Since this card asks what the people did there, covering only the incense leaves out part of the very conduct for which the houses would be defiled in verse 13.

The walkthrough covers the call to turn from wickedness but never includes the LORD's promise in verse 3 to forgive their iniquity and sin. That promise is a central part of why the scroll is written, and no later card supplies it.

Marking this statement false only tells the baker that Jehoiakim will not receive the described honorable burial. No card teaches the verse's actual judgment: his body will be thrown out and exposed to heat by day and frost by night.

The walkthrough ends by asking only whom the LORD will pursue. No card tells the rest of Lamentations 3:66, that He will exterminate them from under His heavens, omitting an important part of the passage's climax.

The fourth case never covers the final result in verse 21: when the righteous man heeds the warning and lives, Ezekiel also saves himself. Cards 10 and 11 cover only the righteous man's response and life, leaving out the watchman's repeated outcome, an important part of the four-case teaching.

The card reduces verse 13 to eating defiled bread among the nations, and no other card says that these are nations to which God will banish the Israelites. That leaves out an important part of the sign's meaning: the coming banishment is something God says He will do.

The walkthrough never covers the final words of verse 17, "in their iniquity." Card 14 mentions only the lack of food and water, and this card asks only about the people wasting away, so the passage's final connection between their wasting away and their iniquity is lost.

The walkthrough leaves out an important part of Ezekiel 14:11: the house of Israel will no longer defile themselves with all their transgressions. Card 13 covers no longer straying from God, and card 14 moves directly to Israel being His people and God being their God, so this part of the LORD's stated purpose is never told or asked.

Ezekiel 47:22 specifically describes foreigners who dwell among Israel and have children. Card 7's answer omits that qualification, and card 8 then describes the foreigners simply as those who live among Israel. The walkthrough never teaches this part of the verse, making residence alone sound like the qualification for the inheritance.

Verse 10 also says that, despite all this, Israel does not seek the LORD. No card tells or asks about that concluding indictment; the false answer here only establishes that Israel does not return to Him.

The stop moves straight to the LORD's roar and never tells verse 10's opening statement that they will walk after the LORD. That omits the important reversal from turning away from Him to following Him.

The correct answer covers only the first part of Joel 1:3. No card includes the children telling their children, and their children telling the next generation, so the verse's important command to pass the account down through successive generations is lost.

Joel 2:23 says that the autumn rains are given 'for your vindication,' but neither card covering that verse mentions this purpose. The stop covers the rains themselves while leaving out an important part of God's promise.

The retelling of Joel 3:3 says only that they bartered a boy away, leaving out that they bartered him for a prostitute. That specific charge is an important part of the nations' exploitation of the LORD's people and helps explain the judgment announced in the passage.

This card uses only the first half of Joel 3:20. Nothing in the walkthrough tells the baker that Jerusalem will continue from generation to generation, so the closing promise concerning Jerusalem is dropped.

The decisive turn in Amos 7:8 is left unclear. Marking this compound statement false does not establish whether Amos does not plead again, whether the LORD does not relent, or both. No other card clearly tells the Lord's actual announcement that He will no longer spare Israel.

This is the only card for Micah 4:5, and rejecting its distorted statement does not tell the baker what the verse actually affirms. The walkthrough moves straight to 4:6 without ever giving the central contrast: though the nations may walk in the names of their gods, Micah's side will walk in the name of the LORD their God forever and ever.

Two important positive facts are never actually taught. Stop 1 card 11 only lets the baker reject keeping the wealth; no card says Zion devotes the gain to the LORD and the wealth to the Lord of all the earth (Micah 4:13). Stop 2 card 7 only rejects shepherding in His own strength; no card says He shepherds in the strength of the LORD and in the majestic name of the LORD His God (Micah 5:4).

The actual outcome in the second half of Micah 5:9 is omitted. Choosing False establishes only that the enemies will not make peace; neither this card nor a later card tells the baker that all the enemies will be cut off.

The resolution of verse 9 is never told. This card stops at Micah enduring the LORD's rage, and card 5 covers only God arguing his case; no card says that God executes justice for him, brings him into the light, or lets him see His righteousness. That leaves an important turn in the passage uncovered.

The important statement in Haggai 2:14 that every work of the people's hands is defiled is never clearly communicated. This card quotes only the people-and-nation clause before moving into its joke, and card 9 asks only about their offerings. The later statement that their work was struck with blight, mildew and hail does not supply the missing detail that their work was defiled.

The card substitutes the kings of Judah for the actual promise, but no card ever tells the baker that Joshua is promised a place among these who are standing here (Zechariah 3:7). Choosing False only rejects the substitute and leaves that part of the verse untaught.

Cards 12-13 cover the lack of compassion and falling into the hands of a neighbor and king, but omit the rest of verse 6: those hands will devastate the land, and the LORD will not deliver it. These concluding judgments are not covered anywhere else.
The walkthrough stops verse 9 after the dying die and the perishing perish. It never covers the verse's concluding judgment that those who remain will devour one another's flesh.

Marking the marketplace statement false only tells the baker where the silver was not thrown. No card states verse 13's actual location: the prophet threw the silver to the potter in the house of the LORD.

Marking this statement false only establishes that John's disciples did not go and tell Herod. No card states what Matthew 14:12 actually says next: they went and informed Jesus. The passage's final action is therefore left untaught.
The walkthrough never identifies the one Instructor as "the Christ." Correctly marking this statement False only rejects Moses, so the key identification in verse 10 remains untold.

The question asks where else people are coming from, but the correct answer omits the region beyond the Jordan from Mark 3:8. No later card covers it, so the walkthrough leaves the list of places incomplete.

The walkthrough covers whom the unforgivable blasphemy is against and that it will never be forgiven, but no card covers the rest of Mark 3:29: "he is guilty of eternal sin." This leaves out a key part of Jesus' warning.

This is the only treatment of Jesus sending the Twelve two by two. Because the statement is false, the baker learns only that they were not sent out one at a time; no card ever supplies the actual detail that Jesus sent them in pairs.

The walkthrough never supplies Gabriel's actual time limit for Zechariah's silence. Card 12 says only that he will be unable to speak, and this card rules out leaving the temple without teaching that the silence lasts until the day the promise comes to pass (Luke 1:20), an important detail of the sign.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

examples: The opening sentence retells the ground being watered from Genesis 2:6, but the card cites only Genesis 2:7. Include verse 6 in the citation or remove that recap.

The opening sentence retells the planted garden from Genesis 2:8, the flowing river from 2:10 and the man's work from 2:15, but the card cites only Genesis 2:18. Adjust the citation or remove the specific recap.
The opening phrase "Hottest part of the day" uses Genesis 18:1, but the card cites only Genesis 18:2-3. The citation should begin with the first verse used, or that detail should be removed.

places.problem: The opening sentence retells the ground being watered from Genesis 2:6, but the card cites only Genesis 2:7. Include verse 6 in the citation or remove that recap.

The opening sentence retells the planted garden from Genesis 2:8, the flowing river from 2:10 and the man's work from 2:15, but the card cites only Genesis 2:18. Adjust the citation or remove the specific recap.
The opening phrase "Hottest part of the day" uses Genesis 18:1, but the card cites only Genesis 18:2-3. The citation should begin with the first verse used, or that detail should be removed.
The opening words "Covenant made" use Genesis 21:27, but the card cites only Genesis 21:28. Its citation should begin with verse 27.

The citation is narrower than the material on the card. The setup that the servant has asked for an answer uses Genesis 24:49, and identifying Bethuel as Rebekah's father uses Genesis 24:47, but the card cites only Genesis 24:50.
The citation stops at Exodus 6:11, but saying that Moses has a question about God's command already tells the reply recorded in Exodus 6:12. The story card's range does not cover every verse it uses.

The picture of Moses "tucked in the rock" uses verse 22, where the LORD puts him in a cleft of the rock and covers him, but the card cites only verse 23. Its citation should run from Exodus 33:22 through Exodus 33:23.
The card cites only Numbers 21:30, but its second sentence also retells the fire that went out from Heshbon, which comes from Numbers 21:28. The citation does not cover every verse the card uses.

The card retells the invitation and bowing down from verse 2 as well as Israel joining in worshiping Baal of Peor in verse 3, but it cites only verse 3. Its citation should cover Numbers 25:2-3, or the verse 2 recap should be removed.
The comments about the cities having to come from somewhere and some tribes being larger than others draw on verse 8, but the card cites only verses 6-7.

The card explicitly reuses the eleven-day journey from verse 2, along with the date in verse 3 and the victories in verse 4, but its citation starts at verse 3. Its story-card citation should be Deuteronomy 1:2-4.
"The tablets are in pieces" retells the shattering of the tablets from Deuteronomy 9:17, but the card cites only Deuteronomy 9:18. Its citation therefore starts later than the first verse it uses.
The card retells both the seven-week count from verse 9 and the Feast of Weeks from verse 10, but it cites only Deuteronomy 16:10. Its citation should begin with verse 9.

The opening also tells that Israel has not yet crossed the Jordan and that the promised land is waiting across it, details drawn from verses 2-3. Citing only verse 1 is narrower than what the card tells.
The card opens by retelling Deuteronomy 32:13 with "Honey from a ROCK," but its citation covers only Deuteronomy 32:16. It therefore does not cite from the first verse the card uses.

The card cites only verse 15, but its second sentence also retells the forty-five-year wait from verse 10 and the completed inheritance from verses 13-14. Replace that recap with a reaction grounded in the rest from war, or otherwise make the card's content and citation agree.
The joke places Kibzaim among the city names, using a detail from Joshua 21:22, but the card cites only Joshua 21:45. The card's citation does not cover that detail.

The card cites only 1 Samuel 2:36, but its opening clause also retells the detail from 1 Samuel 2:29 that Eli's house fattened itself on the best offerings. The citation does not cover everything the card uses.
The card retells both Dagon's first fall in verse 3 and his second fall and damage in verse 4, but it cites only verse 4. Its citation should cover 1 Samuel 5:3-4.
The card retells the seven months in Philistine territory from 6:1 and the cart ride from 6:12-14, but cites only 7:1. Its citation is narrower than the verses it uses.
The card tells David's lament from verse 17, but it also tells that he gives an order about it, which comes from verse 18. Citing only 2 Samuel 1:17 is too narrow; the card uses 2 Samuel 1:17-18.

The card uses verse 1 for "Two questions, two answers" and for the destination Hebron, as well as verse 2 for David going there, but it cites only 2 Samuel 2:2. Its citation should span 2 Samuel 2:1-2.
The opening clause places Absalom in Geshur, drawing on verse 38 and also verse 37, but the card cites only verse 39. Its citation therefore does not begin with the first verse it uses.
The sentence "Then Absalom tells him what he thinks of his case" already uses verse 3, but the card cites only verse 2.

The card retells David's promise from verse 4, that he would do whatever the Gibeonites asked, as well as their request in verse 6. Citing only verse 6 is too narrow; the story card's range should run from verse 4 through verse 6.

Calling Rizpah's son another Mephibosheth and observing that there are two Mephibosheths uses both Jonathan's son in verse 7 and Rizpah's son in verse 8. The citation to verse 8 alone does not cover the whole observation.

Identifying Rizpah as the mother of Armoni and Mephibosheth uses verse 8, while the seven falling together and Rizpah spreading out sackcloth come from verses 9-10. The cited range of 2 Samuel 21:9-10 is therefore too narrow.
The card cites only 1 Kings 6:1, but that verse does not say Solomon was David's son. That relationship appears later in 1 Kings 6:12, so the citation does not cover everything the card tells.
The first sentence retells Elijah's water and twice-a-day deliveries from 1 Kings 17:6, but the card cites only 17:7. The citation should begin with the first verse the card uses.
The second sentence retells the people's earlier silence from 1 Kings 18:21, but the card cites only 1 Kings 18:39.
The closing sentence retells the cloud as small as a hand from 1 Kings 18:44, but the card cites only 1 Kings 18:45.

The opening sentence, "Everybody's chopping," retells the tree-cutting from 2 Kings 6:4, while the axe-head moment comes from 6:5. Citing only 2 Kings 6:5 is narrower than the verses the card uses; the citation should begin at 6:4.
The opening sentence, "Baal's gone from Israel," retells verse 28, but the card cites only 2 Kings 10:29. Its citation should begin with verse 28.

The card says that Gad is given a message to carry to David, which uses the "Go and tell David" instruction in 1 Chronicles 21:10. Its citation covers only 21:9, so it is narrower than the verses the card uses.
The card reuses the troop placement from verse 2 (“Troops in every fortified city?”) but cites only verse 3. Its citation should begin with the first verse it uses.
The joke places the gathering in Hezekiah's first month, which uses 2 Chronicles 29:3, but the card cites only verse 4. The citation is too narrow for the material the card uses.
"Mocked up north" retells the response in verse 10, but the card cites only verse 12. The citation does not cover all the passage content the card uses.
The opening clause, "The people are healed," retells verse 20, but the card cites only verse 21. Either that recap needs to be removed or the citation must account for the verse actually used.

The card reuses verse 20 when it calls Josiah the king who set the temple in order, but it cites only verse 24. The citation does not cover everything the card tells; the callback could instead be removed so the card relies only on verse 24.
The second sentence retells Nehemiah's wine service in 2:1 and his safe-passage and timber requests in 2:7-8, but the card cites only 2:9. Its citation does not cover all the verses the card uses.
The opening sentence tells that four messengers came one right after another, drawing on the messenger reports in Job 1:14-19. Citing only Job 1:20 makes the card's range too narrow.

This story card tells both the earlier detail about God's lamp shining above Job's head from Job 29:3 and the new statement from Job 30:26, but it cites only Job 30:26. Its citation does not cover all the Scripture the card uses.
The detail about fourteen animals uses the seven bulls and seven rams from verse 8, but the card cites only verse 9. The citation needs to cover verses 8-9.

The card uses both the tree by the water from Psalm 1:3 and the chaff driven by the wind from Psalm 1:4, but it cites only Psalm 1:4. Its citation should cover the verses it actually uses, beginning at Psalm 1:3.
The card retells and interprets the grass and water from verse 2 before introducing verse 3, but its citation covers only verse 3.

The observation "He opened with it" uses Psalm 26:1 as well as Psalm 26:11, but the card cites only Psalm 26:11. The wording or citation needs to change so the citation covers exactly what the card uses.

The card retells the retreat and plunder from verse 10 and the mockery from verses 13-16, but cites only Psalm 44:17. Its citation needs to span the earlier material it uses through verse 17, rather than covering only the newest verse.
The card repeats that power belongs to God, which comes from Psalm 62:11, but cites only Psalm 62:12. Its citation is too narrow for the verses it uses.
The card cites only verse 12, but its observation that David "asked for an undivided heart" also uses verse 11.
The card cites only verse 16, but its statement that David started the prayer "poor and needy" also uses verse 1.
The closing sentence introduces Israel's king, which comes from verse 18, but the card cites only verse 17. Its citation should cover Psalm 89:17-18.
The statement that Ethan stops describing and starts asking moves into verse 46, but the card cites only verse 45. Its citation should cover Psalm 89:45-46.
The card cites only verse 10, but its statement that the psalm now tells you why also uses the 'Because' clause in verse 9. Its citation does not include every verse the card uses.

The card cites only Psalm 95:6, but it also retells verse 5's statements about the sea and dry land and reaches back to the mountain peaks in verse 4. Its citation is narrower than the material it uses.
The card retells both the opening "Hallelujah" from verse 1 and the closing praise from verse 10, but it cites only Psalm 111:10.

The card cites only Psalm 131:3, but it also tells details from Psalm 130:7, Psalm 130:1, and Psalm 131:1: the earlier call to hope, the song beginning in the depths, and the song beginning with a heart that is not proud.
The opening sentence retells verse 4's refusal to feast on the wicked men's delicacies before the card moves to verse 5. Citing only Psalm 141:5 is therefore too narrow; the card uses Psalm 141:4-5.
The card retells verse 4 with “Nobody on his right, nobody caring for his soul,” as well as telling verse 5, but it cites only Psalm 142:5. The citation should cover Psalm 142:4-5.
The card uses both verse 1, where the psalm opens with "Hallelujah!", and verse 10, where it closes with the same word, but it cites only Psalm 146:10.

The card retells Proverbs 3:19 when it says the father has just said the LORD founded the earth by wisdom, but its citation is only Proverbs 3:21. The citation does not run from the first verse the card uses to the last.

The card cites only Proverbs 9:14, but it also states that Wisdom called from those heights, which uses Proverbs 9:3, and that she carved seven pillars, which uses Proverbs 9:1. The citation does not cover everything the card tells.

Saying “that line again” uses Proverbs 10:8 as well as Proverbs 10:10, since the earlier line is “foolish lips will come to ruin” in verse 8. The card's citation of only Proverbs 10:10 is narrower than the verses it uses.

The card explicitly compares Proverbs 10:11 with Proverbs 10:6 when it says the second half is “word for word from verse 6,” but its citation covers only verse 11. It should run from verse 6, the first verse used, through verse 11.

The second sentence retells part of verse 20 by saying that the teacher points out a crowd his son should stay away from, but the card cites only verse 19. Since the card uses verses 19-20, its citation stops one verse too early.

The citation Proverbs 27:27 is too narrow. Besides retelling verse 27, the card summarizes the earlier command to look after the flock and the resulting provision in "Look after the flock and the flock looks after you," drawing on verses 23-27.
The sentence "God sent out a call to weep" retells Isaiah 22:12, but the card cites only Isaiah 22:13. The card uses both verses, so its citation should be Isaiah 22:12-13.

The card explicitly retells the offer of repentance and rest and the people's rejection of it from Isaiah 30:15, then tells their response about horses from verse 16. Citing only Isaiah 30:16 is too narrow; the card uses Isaiah 30:15-16.
The card cites only Isaiah 31:2, but its opening sentence also uses the chariots from Isaiah 31:1. Its citation does not run from the first verse it uses.
The card cites only Isaiah 31:5, but "The lion's gone" also uses the lion picture from Isaiah 31:4. The cited range omits the earlier verse the card uses.
The opening sentence retells the deserted roads from Isaiah 33:8 and the mourning land from Isaiah 33:9, but the card cites only Isaiah 33:10. The citation is narrower than the verses the card uses.

The opening sentence retells Isaiah 42:20, that the servant sees many things but does not keep watch, yet the card cites only Isaiah 42:21. If that sentence remains, the citation needs to begin at verse 20.
The observation that this is the third call to listen uses verses 12 and 14 as well as verse 16, but the card cites only verse 16.
The callback to peace like a river uses verse 18, but the card cites only verse 22.
The card cites only Isaiah 49:18, but it also retells Zion's complaint from Isaiah 49:14 when it says that she said she had been forgotten. Its citation does not cover everything the card tells.

The card retells the mute watchdogs of Isaiah 56:10 and identifies the shepherds of Isaiah 56:11 before moving to Isaiah 56:12, but it cites only Isaiah 56:12. Its citation should span Isaiah 56:10-12.
The opening clause, 'Peace to those far and near,' tells Isaiah 57:19, but the card cites only Isaiah 57:20. Its citation should be Isaiah 57:19-20.
The card tells Jeremiah 9:8 but also retells the earlier image of tongues bent like bows from Jeremiah 9:3. Citing only Jeremiah 9:8 is narrower than the verses the card uses.

The card retells the gentle-lamb image from Jeremiah 11:19, but its citation is only Jeremiah 12:3-4 and it gives no reference for 11:19. The citation therefore does not cover everything the card tells.
The card explicitly uses the lion from verse 8 and the bird from verse 9 alongside the vineyard from verse 10, but it cites only Jeremiah 12:10. The citation should cover Jeremiah 12:8-10.
The description "the man who put the prophet in the stocks" uses the action from verse 2, but the card cites only verse 6. The citation does not cover everything the card tells.

The card places Shemaiah among the exiles in Babylon, but Jeremiah 29:24-25 does not state that detail. It is supported later in the passage, so the cited range does not cover everything the card tells.

The last sentence says that the word starts with a job for Jeremiah, which uses Jeremiah 30:2, but the card cites only Jeremiah 30:1. The citation should extend through the verse that mentions the job.

The second sentence moves into Jeremiah 31:1 by saying that the LORD then speaks about what will be true at that time, but the card cites only Jeremiah 30:24. Its citation should include every verse it uses.
The teaser about something that 'shows up on time, every time' draws on the appointed day-and-night cycle in verse 20, but the card cites only verse 19.
The statement that Babylon's army had surrounded Jerusalem uses Jeremiah 37:5, but the card cites only Jeremiah 37:19-20. Its citation does not cover every Bible fact it tells.
"The walls are open" retells the breach from Jeremiah 39:2, but the card cites only Jeremiah 39:3. The citation is too narrow for everything the card tells.
By saying that the LORD speaks "again" and that the command occurs "Twice in a row," the card uses both Jeremiah 46:27 and Jeremiah 46:28, but it cites only Jeremiah 46:28.
The card tells verse 4, but its second sentence also uses verse 5 when it says that the LORD then says something about Israel and Judah. The citation therefore ends one verse too early.
The second sentence retells Ezekiel 21:20 by identifying Rabbah as the city at the end of the other road, but the card cites only Ezekiel 21:28.

The closing sentence retells the earlier appearances of Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, and Sidon, beginning in Ezekiel 32:22, but the card cites only Ezekiel 32:32. Its citation does not cover everything the card tells.
The second sentence retells Hosea 11:1 by saying Egypt is the place the LORD called Israel out of, but the card's citation covers only Hosea 11:5.
The closing clause about the prophet reaching out to the LORD retells Joel's call in Joel 1:19, but the card cites only Joel 1:20. The citation is too narrow for everything the card uses.

The card cites only Jonah 2:7, but its second sentence also retells Jonah 2:4 when it says Jonah had said he would look toward God's temple once more. The citation is narrower than the verses the card uses; following the first-to-last rule, it would be Jonah 2:4-7.

The opening sentence reuses the net from Micah 7:2, the bribe from Micah 7:3 and the thorn from Micah 7:4 before turning to Micah 7:7. Citing only Micah 7:7 leaves out the earlier verses the card uses.
The card says that the LORD's next word through Haggai is a question, which uses Haggai 1:4, but its citation stops at Haggai 1:3. The citation needs to extend through Haggai 1:4.
The card retells the four horns scattering God's people from Zechariah 1:19, but its verses field cites only Zechariah 1:20. The citation should cover Zechariah 1:19-20.

The card cites only Zechariah 9:17, but its opening sentence also retells the waterless pit from Zechariah 9:11 and the jewels in a crown from Zechariah 9:16. Its citation does not cover everything the card tells.

The card retells the Magi asking where the King of the Jews is, which comes from Matthew 2:2, as well as Herod hearing the news in 2:3. Citing only Matthew 2:3 is too narrow; the card uses Matthew 2:2-3.
Identifying these as the prophet's words uses Matthew 2:5, while the quoted prophecy comes from 2:6. The citation of only Matthew 2:6 is too narrow; the card uses Matthew 2:5-6.
The statement that the man came in lying on a mat retells Matthew 9:2, but the card cites only Matthew 9:7. Its citation therefore does not cover every passage verse the card uses.

The card cites only Matthew 13:8, but its opening also retells the path, rocky ground and thorns and their unsuccessful results from Matthew 13:4-7. Its citation does not begin with the earliest verse the card uses.

The card retells that the crowd knows Jesus's mother and brothers, which comes from Matthew 13:55, as well as the sisters and repeated question in verse 56. Citing only Matthew 13:56 is too narrow for the material the card uses.
The sentence "She came in asking about seats" retells the mother's request from Matthew 20:21, but the card cites only Matthew 20:22. Its citation should begin with the first verse it uses.
"The sea goes quiet" retells the calm from Mark 4:39, but the card cites only Mark 4:40. Its citation does not begin with the first verse it uses.
The flat, calm sea retells Mark 4:39, while the disciples' fearful question comes from Mark 4:41. Citing only Mark 4:41 omits the earlier verse the card uses.

The opening clause retells Jesus taking the little girl by the hand and her getting up, which is Mark 5:41-42, but the card cites only Mark 6:5. Its citation is narrower than the Bible content it tells.

The card retells Jesus' warning about leaven from Mark 8:15 before covering the disciples' discussion and Jesus' questions in Mark 8:16-17. Its citation starts at Mark 8:16 instead of the first verse it uses, so the range should be Mark 8:15-17.

The opening sentence retells the darkened sun and moon and the falling stars from Mark 13:24-25 before introducing verse 26, but the card cites only Mark 13:26. Its used range is Mark 13:24-26, unless the retelling is removed.
The card uses the rebuke from Mark 16:14 as well as the mission in Mark 16:15, but it cites only Mark 16:15.
The closing sentence retells the Eleven's earlier unbelief from Mark 16:14, but the card cites only Mark 16:20. The citation does not cover all the passage facts the card uses.

rule.text: A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

examples: Cards 2, 3, 4 and 9 all require facts not supplied by the earlier cards: Eve's name, the reason for that name, the material of the garments and what God stations at Eden. Only cards 7 and 10 offer a reasonable basis for an informed pick, so most of this stop's choices rely on guessing.

Three of the stop's five choice cards depend on discovery guesses rather than reasoning. Card 5 gives no indication of what Lamech will announce, card 6 gives three numbers that all satisfy the setup that Lamech “tops” sevenfold, and card 10 gives no basis for predicting what began in Enosh's days. Consequently, most of this stop's choices are not informed guesses.

Too many choices require luck rather than a reasoned pick. Cards 4, 9, 10, 12, 17 and 18 ask for facts that cannot be reasoned out or eliminated from the earlier cards: the direction east, the exact cave, the field-and-Sarah statement, Beer-lahai-roi, the Havilah-to-Shur span and hostility toward the brothers. That is more than a few discovery questions, leaving much of the stop a guessing game.

places.problem: Cards 2, 3, 4 and 9 all require facts not supplied by the earlier cards: Eve's name, the reason for that name, the material of the garments and what God stations at Eden. Only cards 7 and 10 offer a reasonable basis for an informed pick, so most of this stop's choices rely on guessing.

Three of the stop's five choice cards depend on discovery guesses rather than reasoning. Card 5 gives no indication of what Lamech will announce, card 6 gives three numbers that all satisfy the setup that Lamech “tops” sevenfold, and card 10 gives no basis for predicting what began in Enosh's days. Consequently, most of this stop's choices are not informed guesses.

Too many choices require luck rather than a reasoned pick. Cards 4, 9, 10, 12, 17 and 18 ask for facts that cannot be reasoned out or eliminated from the earlier cards: the direction east, the exact cave, the field-and-Sarah statement, Beer-lahai-roi, the Havilah-to-Shur span and hostility toward the brothers. That is more than a few discovery questions, leaving much of the stop a guessing game.

Most of this stop's choices are discoveries rather than informed guesses. Cards 2, 4, 5, 7, 12, 13, 14 and 16 ask for the water, flies, houses, Goshen, Pharaoh's exact offer, Moses' reason, the three-day wilderness journey and Moses' warning without earlier cards supplying a basis to reason those out. That is 8 of 13 choices, so the stop becomes a guessing game.

Most of this stop's choices require luck or prior knowledge rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. The three days in card 2, the bitterness in card 4, Moses' response in card 6, the diseases in card 10, and the exact springs and palm trees in card 13 are all unrevealed details with no sufficient clues in their setups. That makes discovery questions the norm in this stop instead of the exception.

Five of the nine choices in this stop (cards 2, 3, 8, 10 and 13) lack a basis in the earlier cards: the baker must guess Aaron's name, whether the workers received a design, whether the waistband was one piece, what the onyx stones bore, and whether the breastpiece matched the ephod's workmanship. That makes most of this stop's choices discovery guesses rather than informed picks.

Discovery questions are the pattern across the walkthrough rather than an occasional exception. For example, stop 1 card 12 gives no clue that the fire is on the ash heap; stop 2 cards 2, 4, 7 and 9 require guesses about animals or blood procedures; and stop 3 cards 4, 7, 8, 10 and 11 provide no basis for reasoning out their answers. A thoughtful baker using only the earlier cards would have to rely on luck for most of these choices.

Five of the stop's eight choices ask for facts the earlier cards do not help the baker reason out: the duration in card 2, clothes washing in card 3, the clean-animal carcass rule in card 8, the reason for holiness in card 12, and the place in card 13. This concentrated run of discovery questions makes the stop a guessing game rather than relying mainly on informed guesses.

Most of this stop's choices are discovery questions rather than informed guesses. Cards 2, 4, 5, 7, 12 and 14 ask for the Sabbath work rule, the kind of bread, the assembly days, the priest's action, the use of leaven and the duration of the statute without earlier cards providing a basis for reasoning out those answers. Only cards 9, 11 and 16 clearly support a reasoned pick.

Most of the choices are luck-based discovery questions rather than informed guesses. For example, cards 8, 10, 11, 12 and 14 ask for the lampstand material, loaf count, row arrangement, frankincense and timing of the bread without earlier cards giving a basis to reason them out. Cards 2, 3 and 7 have the same problem, so discovery questions make up most of the stop rather than just a few.

At least five of the nine choice cards are discovery questions with no basis for a reasoned pick in the earlier cards: card 2 asks the trumpets' purposes, cards 6 and 7 ask for the east and south camps, card 10 asks who will sound the trumpets, and card 12 asks for God's specific promise in battle. Even counting every other choice as informed, only four of nine are informed guesses, so discovery questions make up too much of the stop.

Cards 2, 6, 9, 11, 13 and 18 ask for details that cannot be reasoned out from anything in the earlier cards. That is six of the eleven choice cards, so discovery questions make up most of the stop instead of only a few.

Discovery questions dominate the stop. Cards 6, 10, 14 and 16 cannot be reasoned out from the earlier cards, and cards 2 and 4 also provide little basis for a reasoned pick. Thus at least half of the eight choices depend on luck or prior Bible knowledge, rather than most choices being informed guesses.

Four of the seven choice cards require luck rather than reasoning from earlier cards: card 5 asks for an unheard city count, card 7 gives no basis for judging the fortifications, card 11 asks for an unheard people group and card 12 asks for an unheard bed material. Discovery questions therefore dominate this stop instead of remaining a few exceptions.

Discovery questions dominate the stop instead of being the exception. Cards 2, 4, 6, 12 and 13 provide no earlier-card basis for reasoning out Joshua, the purpose involving children, life, Moses' death or Aaron, and card 11 likewise asks for the unrevealed name Canaan. That makes at least six of the ten choice cards dependent on guessing a new detail rather than most choices being informed guesses.

Discovery questions are overused. Cards 2, 10, 13, 14, 17 and 18 ask for details the earlier cards do not help the baker reason out: Gibeon's size and might, the all-night surprise march, the hailstones, the comparative death toll, the Book of Jashar and the length of the sun's delay. These picks depend largely on luck or prior recall rather than the walkthrough's setup.

Discovery questions dominate the stop. Cards 2, 4, 6 and 11, along with the blanks in cards 5 and 8, ask for facts that cannot be inferred from the earlier cards. At least six of the eight choices therefore depend on outside knowledge or luck rather than informed picks.

Most of the choices are not informed guesses. Cards 2, 8, 13, 15 and 17 depend on discovering details that the earlier cards have not supplied, while cards 4 and 7 ask for unseen wording. Only cards 10, 12, 16 and 19 clearly give the baker enough context to reason toward an answer. Add context or replace some questions so that discovery questions remain the exception.

Too many choice cards depend on luck rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. For example, the baker has no basis for choosing Hebron in card 3, Caleb's daughter as the reward in card 7, whether anyone captures the city in card 8, springs of water in card 11, or whether Judah drives out the Jebusites in card 15. These discovery questions account for at least five of the nine choice cards, rather than being the allowed few.

Too many choices depend on discovering an unforeseeable detail rather than reasoning from earlier cards. Cards 4, 8, 10, 17, 18 and 19 provide no earlier basis for inferring the supplies, the mob's target, the old man's offer, where the pieces are sent, the starting point of the comparison or the call to action. Six discovery questions out of ten are more than the allowed few.

Cards 2, 3, 6, 9, 12 and 18 require unseen names, events or details that cannot be reasoned out from the earlier cards. Discovery questions therefore make up half of the stop's twelve choices, rather than just a few, and most choice cards are not informed guesses.

Too much of this stop depends on luck rather than informed guesses. The preceding cards give no basis for distinguishing the answers about thunder in card 2, the name Ebenezer in card 6, the Amorites in card 10, or Ramah in card 12. Those unrevealed-detail questions account for half of the stop's eight choices, so discovery questions are not limited to a few while most choices remain reasoned picks.

Too many choices depend on discovering a fact rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Cards 2, 6, 10, 14, 16 and 18 provide no earlier-card basis for working out the Exodus reminder, Benjamin, Saul's height, the writing of the scroll, Saul's companions or Saul's silence. That makes six of the ten choice cards discovery questions, so most choices are not informed guesses.

Too many choices depend on discovery rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Cards 5, 6 and 10 provide no basis for choosing David, Amalek or not eating; cards 13 and 18 likewise give no contextual basis for predicting Saul's immediate refusal or whether the group stays until morning. This is more than a few discovery questions and leaves only about half the stop's choices reasonably informed.

Too many choices depend on facts the earlier cards have not supplied rather than on reasoning: whether David inquires about the woman (card 4), the additional detail about Bathsheba (card 5), where Uriah sleeps (card 11), what Uriah says about the ark (card 14), whether David sends him back that day (card 16), and whether the drunken Uriah goes home (card 18). These are more than a few discovery questions, so most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses.

Discovery questions are too frequent. Stop 1 cards 2, 4, 6, 12, 15 and 16 ask for unrevealed decisions or reactions without enough earlier-card context to reason out one answer, and stop 2 cards 6 and 12 likewise depend on luck. For example, the baker has no basis for reasoning out the ten concubines, the countryside's reaction, the ark's return, David's statement about it, David calling Hushai a burden, or the exact timing of Hushai's arrival. This goes beyond a few discovery questions alongside mostly informed guesses.

Discovery questions are not limited to a few here. Cards 8, 11, 12, 15, 18 and 19 quiz unrevealed details, and card 2 likewise gives no passage-based basis for choosing its answer. Most of the stop's choices consequently depend on prior knowledge, answer wording or luck rather than reasoning from the earlier cards.

Cards 3, 5, 11 and 13 provide no preceding setup from which their answers can be reasoned: the third thing Solomon did not request, God's uniqueness promise, Solomon's return to Jerusalem and his closing feast. Four of the stop's seven choice cards are therefore discovery questions, so informed guesses do not make up most of the stop.

Most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses. Cards 2, 5, 7, 8, 11 and 15 require facts that the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out, and card 9 is likewise an unsupported true-or-false prediction. Only cards 13 and 16 clearly provide a reasoning basis, so discovery questions make up most of the stop rather than a few exceptions.

Too much of this stop depends on guessing unrevealed facts. Cards 2, 4, 5, 7, 11 and 15 ask for God's promise, the officers He will use, who starts the battle, the exact troop count, Ben-hadad's order and Ben-hadad's fate without enough earlier context to reason out those picks. Consequently, most of the stop's choices feel like discovery questions or luck rather than informed guesses.

Too many choices depend on discovering an unrevealed detail rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Cards 4, 5, 7, 11 and 12 provide no sufficient basis for inferring mercy, the sackcloth and ropes, Ahab's unexpected brother language, the restored cities or the marketplaces. This is more than the allowed few discovery questions.

Most choice cards require luck or prior Bible knowledge rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Examples include Jehoshaphat's reign length, the high places, his peace with Israel, whom he banishes, the gold at Ophir, the ships' fate, his refusal of Ahaziah, his successor, Ahaziah's reign length, Jeroboam's identity and Baal. These discovery questions dominate both stops instead of being the allowed few.

Most of this stop's choices are unaided discovery guesses. Cards 3, 5, 8, 10 and 12 ask for Manasseh's name, the particular judgment, Josiah's response to Neco, the place of Josiah's death and his successor, but the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out any of those answers.

Most choices are not informed guesses. The earlier cards give no way to reason out the mother's stated reason (card 3), the content or outcome of the prayer (cards 5 and 7), the land's condition or former inhabitants (cards 12–13), or the destination, enemy and final settlement (cards 17–19). This goes beyond a few discovery questions among mostly informed choices.

Too many choices depend on facts withheld from the preceding cards. Cards 2, 6, 8, 10 and 15 provide no basis for reasoning out singers, Obed-edom's house, the exact sacrifice, David's clothing or Michal's reaction. Discovery picks therefore dominate this stop instead of most choices being informed guesses.

Too many of this stop's choices depend on luck rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Cards 4, 9, 11 and 15 ask for unrevealed details about who receives food, what the song says next and which land God promises. Card 18 then asks for the specific way the LORD protects the wanderers, although card 17 establishes only that He prevents oppression. Even allowing card 2 as a discovery question, five of the nine choices are not informed guesses.

Too many choices require luck or prior Bible knowledge because the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out the answer. Stop 1 cards 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 16, and stop 2 cards 7, 9, 11 and 14, all ask for unrevealed details without a meaningful setup. That is 10 of the 17 choice cards, so discovery questions are not merely a small exception.

Cards 2, 6, 8, 9 and 12 require facts that cannot be reasoned out from the earlier cards: the sons' ministry, what Jeduthun says while playing, how Heman received his sons, and two exact totals. That makes most of the stop's eight choice cards discovery questions rather than informed guesses.

Cards 2, 4, 5, 11 and 16 ask for the reign length, the place Jotham avoided, the people's behavior, the later payments and the burial city without giving any earlier-card basis for reasoning out those answers. That is at least five of the nine choice cards, so discovery guesses make up most of the stop rather than just a few exceptions.

Discovery questions are used too often. Stop 1 cards 7-8 and stop 2 cards 2-3 and 8-9 provide no earlier-card basis for reasoning out the feast, the daily offering schedule, the sea route, Cyrus's authorization, the instruments, or David. The consecutive instrument and David blanks are especially dependent on luck, taking the walkthrough beyond the allowed few discovery questions.

Most of this stop's choices require luck rather than an informed guess. Cards 2, 3, 5, 6, 11 and 14 ask for details that the earlier cards neither supply nor provide enough context to reason out, and cards 8 and 10 are also largely discovery questions. This exceeds the allowed few discovery questions.

The guessing problem extends beyond the blanks. Stop 1 cards 4, 8, 14 and 16 provide no earlier setup from which to infer the requested blessing, the three things the king rides for, the harps' location, or whether the queen stands at his left or right. Stop 2 cards 2 and 8 likewise provide no basis for inferring what the daughter must forget or who accompanies the princess. Together with the wording blanks, discovery questions make up most of the choices rather than the allowed few.

Cards 2, 6, 7, 11, 14 and 17 provide no earlier-card basis for reliably distinguishing the right answer from the alternatives. That makes six of the eleven choices dependent on luck or prior Bible knowledge, so discovery questions dominate instead of remaining a few.

Too many of this stop's choices depend on discovering unseen wording rather than reasoning from earlier cards. Card 2 gives no clue to the scope of the group called to sing, card 4 gives no clue to the frequency, card 9 does not establish why the gods must be idols rather than angels or kings, and card 11 provides no context for evaluating the sanctuary statement. That makes four of the six choice cards uninformed discoveries, so most choices in the stop are not informed guesses.

Most of this stop's choices are not informed guesses. Cards 2, 4, 6, 8, 11 and 13 withhold the target detail without providing earlier context from which to reason it out, leaving six of the eight choices dependent on luck or prior Bible knowledge.

This stop relies on discovery questions more than informed guesses. Cards 2, 6, 8, 11, 15 and 18 ask for the firstborn, the dividing of the sea, Pharaoh's fate, the kings' names, when the LORD remembered us, and what He gives every creature without earlier cards providing a basis for choosing among the answers. Six of the ten choices therefore depend on prior knowledge or luck.

Too many choices depend on guessing an unrevealed detail. Cards 2, 4 and 6 are detail-discovery questions, while cards 11, 15 and 16 also lack enough context for a reasoned answer. Consequently, most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses, and the discoveries amount to more than a few.

The stop repeatedly pauses just before an unseen detail or the unseen second half of a verse. Cards 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 13 and 14 do not provide enough earlier context to reason out the stated answer over the alternatives. For example, card 4 supplies none of the three proposed reasons in card 5. Only cards 9, 11 and 16 are clearly informed guesses, so the discovery questions are not limited to a few.

The stop relies too heavily on discovery and luck. Cards 4, 6, 7, 9 and 17 ask for names, events, agents or outcomes that cannot be inferred from the earlier cards; together with card 2's wording guess, they make six of the eleven choices uninformed rather than leaving most choices as informed guesses.

Cards 2, 4 and 6 require discovering details that the earlier cards do not help the baker infer: Seir, whether the cry is repeated and what the watchman answers. Even treating cards 3 and 8 as reasoned picks, three of the five choice cards are discovery questions, so most choice cards are not informed guesses.

Five of the nine choice cards (3, 5, 8, 10 and 17) require unseen details that cannot be reasoned from the earlier cards: whether the word continues after Josiah, the exile, the nations, Jeremiah's objection and the rest of the job list. That leaves only four informed guesses, so most of this stop's choices are discoveries rather than informed guesses.

Discovery guesses dominate this stop. Card 2 asks for wine with no clue, card 6 asks whether the Rechabites drink before their command is known, card 7 introduces Jonadab only in the answers, and card 10 asks for Jonadab's reason without context. That is four of the stop's seven choice cards, so most are not informed guesses a baker can reason out from the earlier cards.

Six of the eight choice cards—2, 4, 5, 7, 9 and 12—ask for details that earlier cards neither supply nor make inferable: the writing material, Baruch's condition, the sorrow added to his pain, whose work is demolished, what Baruch is seeking and what the disaster strikes. Discovery questions consequently dominate the stop instead of remaining a few exceptions among mostly informed guesses.

Cards 3, 7, 9, 13 and 15 ask for direct revelation, a human form, human hands, the three animal faces or the spirit's leading before the earlier cards provide a sufficient basis for choosing. Five of the nine choices depend on discovery rather than reasoning, so informed guesses are not the dominant pattern.

Discovery questions recur beyond a small exception. For example, the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out a year in stop 1 card 8, Judah in stop 1 card 10, prophesying in stop 1 card 14, eating at set times in stop 2 card 4, or God's concession in stop 2 card 11. The location in stop 2 card 7 is likewise unrevealed. This recurring pattern makes too much of Prep depend on luck or prior knowledge rather than reasoned picks from the setups.

Cards 2, 4, 8, 10 and 16 require facts that the earlier cards do not help the baker infer: the lioness, the cub's violence, Egypt, the choice of another cub and Babylon. Five of the stop's nine choices are therefore discovery guesses, leaving only four informed guesses, so the permitted exceptions have become the majority.

Cards 2, 4 and 6 are all discovery questions: the earlier cards give no basis for choosing Rabbah, seeking an omen, or Jerusalem rather than Rabbah. Three of the stop's five choices therefore come down to luck, so most of this stop's choices are not informed guesses and the discovery questions go beyond the allowed few.

Most of this stop's choices are not informed guesses. Cards 2, 3, 9, 10, 16 and 17 ask for the idols, the absence of a prince, the broken body part, the lack of treatment, the sword's owner and the mortally wounded simile before the earlier cards give any basis for reasoning to those details. Six discovery guesses out of ten leaves only four informed choices.

Three of the stop's five choices depend on luck rather than an informed guess. Card 2 gives no basis for choosing what the people say, card 4 gives no basis for knowing whether they practice Ezekiel's words, and card 6 asks what their hearts pursue after the setup merely says they are chasing "something else." That makes most of this stop a guessing game rather than allowing only a few discovery questions.

Discovery questions dominate this stop. Cards 2, 4, 5, 9, 12 and 13 ask for unrevealed details that cannot be inferred from the earlier cards: Gabriel's name, what he gives Daniel, when the answer went out, the endpoint of the timeline, what happens to the Messiah, and whether the coming prince's people destroy the city and sanctuary. That is six of the stop's nine choice cards, leaving most picks dependent on luck or prior knowledge rather than reasoning from the walkthrough.

Five of the nine choice cards (4, 6, 10, 12 and 13) require outside knowledge or luck: the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out Judah's response, Ephraim's action with Assyria and Egypt, what Jacob grabs, what Jacob does after prevailing, or the location Bethel. This concentration makes most of the stop's choices discovery questions rather than informed guesses.

Too many choices require guessing details that the earlier cards have not supplied or made inferable. Cards 4-5 ask for two unrevealed parts of Amaziah's report, cards 11-12 ask about Amos's background and then his occupation without a useful clue, and cards 7 and 19 add further blind detail guesses. Discovery questions make up about half of the stop, including two consecutive pairs, rather than remaining a few exceptions among mostly informed guesses.

Too many choices are discoveries or coin flips for informed guesses to be the majority. Stop 1 card 5 asks about redemption in Babylon right after only the destination was established; stop 1 card 11 gives no basis for deciding who gets the wealth; stop 1 card 13 introduces the struck judge only in the question; and stop 2 card 3 introduces the ruler's eternal origins only in the question. Added to the picture, destination and town discovery questions, a baker using only the earlier cards must guess on about half of the choices.

Most choices are discoveries rather than informed guesses. Cards 4, 6, 10, 15 and 17 offer little or no basis in the earlier cards for reasoning out the answer; together with the unrevealed-detail blanks in cards 2 and 9, that makes seven of the ten choices dependent on prior knowledge or luck. Discovery questions therefore dominate the stop instead of being the few exceptions.

Discovery questions dominate the stop. Cards 2, 3, 6, 11, 13, 14, 16, 18 and 19 provide no earlier-card basis for reasoning out the answer, leaving only cards 7, 8 and 9 clearly grounded in what the baker has already learned.

Discovery questions are too frequent to remain the allowed exception. Stop 1 cards 2, 5, 8 and 9 ask for details that cannot be inferred from the earlier cards, and stop 2 cards 2, 6 and 11 likewise ask for unrevealed facts without an inferential setup. Consequently, too much of the walkthrough depends on prior knowledge or luck rather than informed reasoning.

Discovery questions make up at least half of the walkthrough rather than a few exceptions. Stop 1 cards 4, 8, 12, 16 and 17, and stop 2 cards 4, 6, 8, 11, 13 and 20, provide no earlier-card basis for reasoning out the answer. For example, the baker has no contextual way to determine who accompanies the LORD, whether the water flows year-round, which feast the survivors celebrate, or whether rain rather than manna or dew will be withheld.

Cards 2, 5, 6 and 7 give no earlier-card basis for choosing their answers: the extent of the healing, what God puts on the Servant, what He proclaims, and whether He quarrels and cries out are all unrevealed details. Four of the stop's seven choice cards are luck-based, including three consecutive guesses at Isaiah's wording, so this stop becomes a guessing game rather than relying mostly on informed guesses.

Most of the stop's choices are discovery questions rather than informed guesses. Before cards 2, 3, 6, 7 and 9, the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out the synagogue, the crowd's astonishment, the carpenter's-son question, Mary's name or whether Jesus's sisters are present. Five of nine choice cards therefore require prior knowledge or luck, which is more than the allowed few discovery questions.

Too many choices depend on luck rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Cards 2, 4, 7, 14 and 16 provide no contextual basis for reasoning out the size of the gathering, the crown's material, the spitting, Golgotha's meaning or whether Jesus drinks after tasting. These five discovery questions outnumber the stop's informed guesses.

The same guessing pattern continues in cards 2, 3, 7, 13 and 14. The earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out casting lots, staying to keep watch, the robbers' identity, the leaders' trust-in-God taunt or whether the robbers join the mockery. Five of the stop's eight choices are therefore discoveries rather than informed guesses.

Discovery or coin-flip picks are too prevalent. Stop 1 cards 2, 4, 8 and 10, and stop 2 cards 2, 3, 7 and 13 withhold the crucial fact without giving earlier-card context from which to reason. These eight of the fourteen choice cards include guesses at the untranslated cry, the sponge's contents, the bystanders' response, the veil's fate and tearing direction, the saints' timing, and Mary Magdalene's presence. Informed guesses therefore do not clearly dominate the walkthrough.

Most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses.
