Card 2 is also a discovery question, while only cards 9 and 10 clearly provide enough setup for a reasoned pick.

Too many choices depend on luck rather than the earlier cards: how Jesus heals (6), the immediate timing (8), the warning's content (10), the priest and Moses details (11), the offering's purpose (12), and whether the man obeys (14) are not inferable from their setups. Six of the ten choice cards are discovery questions, so most choices are not informed guesses.

Too much of this stop relies on discovery rather than informed choices. Cards 2, 4, 5, 13, 14 and 18 require details that the earlier cards do not supply or imply: six of the stop's eleven choice cards, leaving most of its choices something other than informed guesses.

Too many choices depend on guessing unrevealed details. Cards 5, 7 and 9 provide no basis for reasoning out spit, incomplete sight or trees. Card 4 is also a guess because card 3 never says that Jesus led the man out of the village before asking whether He healed him in the village. That leaves only half of the stop's eight choice cards as informed guesses, rather than most of them.

Discovery questions dominate the walkthrough rather than remaining a few exceptions. For example, the name's origin (stop 1 card 2), the sacrifice (stop 1 card 7), Simeon's revelation (stop 1 card 9), what the Child is appointed to cause (stop 2 card 3), Anna's whereabouts (stop 2 card 10), the family's destination (stop 2 card 16), and Jesus' wisdom and grace (stop 2 card 18) all require new information that cannot be worked out from the earlier cards. Together with the other unsupported choices, this leaves most choices dependent on discovery or luck rather than reasoning.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

examples: The card cites only Genesis 18:31, but its recap also uses the earlier fifty, forty-five, forty, and thirty steps from Genesis 18:24-30. The citation does not span the passage material the card uses.

The statement that Lot is asking to change the destination tells the substance of his request in Genesis 19:19-20, but the card cites only Genesis 19:18, which contains just his opening objection. Either the citation must include the verses used or the line must stay within verse 18.
The card explicitly counts both of Jacob's blessings with "one more time" and "TWO blessings," so it uses Genesis 47:7 as well as Genesis 47:10. Its citation includes only Genesis 47:10.

The card tells the total in verse 46 and the excluded tribe in verse 47, but it does not tell verse 44's twelve assisting leaders or verse 45's age, army and family qualifications. Its citation of Numbers 1:44-47 therefore starts wider than the content it uses.
The card cites only verse 28, but its closing phrase "one goat" also retells the offering prescribed in verse 27. Its citation is therefore narrower than the verses it uses.
The opening sentence retells Numbers 20:11 with "Water's gushing, everybody's drinking," but the card cites only Numbers 20:12. The citation does not begin with the first verse the card uses.
The final sentence tells Balaam's move into the subject of spells and divination, which comes from Numbers 23:23, but the card cites only Numbers 23:22.
The claim that the LORD says this a "third time" uses the earlier commands in verses 6 and 7, but the card cites only verses 8-9. The citation does not cover every verse the card uses.
The sentence beginning "At the start" retells the LORD's promise from verse 5, but the card cites only verse 17. Its citation therefore omits a verse it uses.
The card cites only Joshua 8:34, but "to the whole crowd" tells the audience identified in Joshua 8:35 as the whole assembly. The citation does not cover every verse the card uses.
The card retells Caleb driving out the three sons of Anak, which comes from Joshua 15:14, but its citation begins at Joshua 15:15. The cited range does not include every verse the card uses.

The opening sentence retells the northern border passing the Jebusites at Jerusalem, which comes from Joshua 15:8, but the card cites only Joshua 15:63. Its citation does not cover all the passage content it uses.

The card tells both about the coming war against Israel (1 Samuel 28:1) and David's appointment as bodyguard (1 Samuel 28:2), but it cites only 1 Samuel 28:2. Its citation should cover 1 Samuel 28:1-2.

The card repeats that Ittai arrived only yesterday, which comes from 2 Samuel 15:20, but its citation starts at verse 21. Since the card also tells verses 21-22, its reference is narrower than the material it uses; it should begin at verse 20 or omit the verse-20 detail.
Calling Huram a craftsman draws on his bronze skill and work in 1 Kings 7:14, but the card cites only 7:13, which says that Solomon sent to bring him from Tyre.
The opening statement that the ark is in its place retells 1 Kings 8:6, but the card cites only 1 Kings 8:10. Its citation does not cover everything the card tells.
The card cites 1 Kings 12:22-23, but its joke also uses the 180,000 warriors from 1 Kings 12:21 without giving that reference. Its citation starts after the first verse it uses.
The opening clause, "With Damascus captured," tells the capture from verse 9, but the card cites only verse 10. If that recapped fact is retained, the citation needs to begin at 2 Kings 16:9.
The card cites only 2 Kings 25:28, but "After thirty-seven years" also uses the length of Jehoiachin's exile from verse 27. The card therefore does not cite every verse it uses.
The clause about the Reubenites' herds pushing them to the edge of the desert retells verse 9, but the card cites only verse 10. Its citation does not cover everything the story card uses.
The phrase "the same king who carried off Beerah" retells verse 6, but the card cites only verse 26. The citation therefore does not cover all the passage material the card uses.

The opening clause, 'All Israel is shouting down below,' retells 1 Chronicles 15:28, while Michal's response comes from verse 29. Citing only verse 29 is too narrow; the card should cite 1 Chronicles 15:28-29.

The closing line uses the morning and evening praise schedule from verse 30 as well as the feast-day service from verse 31, but the card cites only verse 31.

The card's only Bible detail, the thirteenth day of Adar, comes from Esther 8:12, but the card cites Esther 8:17 and adds nothing from that verse. The citation does not match the content used.
The second sentence also retells the opening petition from Psalm 20:1, but the card cites only Psalm 20:9. The citation therefore does not cover all the verses the card uses.
The card retells the waters, fire and shaking ground from Psalm 29:3, 7 and 8, but its citation is only Psalm 29:10. The citation therefore does not cover everything the card uses.

The card cites only Psalm 50:14, but its second sentence says that God makes a promise for the hard days, which tells part of verse 15. The story-card citation should therefore extend through verse 15.

The line "An enemy David can take" reuses Psalm 55:12, where David says he could endure an enemy's insult, but the card cites only Psalm 55:13-14. The citation needs to include verse 12, or that clause needs to be removed.

The card cites only verse 1, but it also says that the singers state why they want the blessing. That purpose is introduced by the purpose clause in verse 2, so the card uses verses 1-2 and its citation is too narrow.

The citation is wider than the story the card tells. Its only specific request is being blotted out of the Book of Life and not listed with the righteous, which is verse 28; it does not tell verse 27's requests to add iniquity to their iniquity and not let them share in God's righteousness.

The card cites only Psalm 78:72, but its second sentence also retells Psalm 78:52, God leading His people out like sheep, and Psalm 78:70-71, God bringing David to shepherd that flock. Its citation does not cover everything the card tells.

The card cites only verse 9, but its closing sentence also uses verse 10 by introducing the picture of four things: loving devotion, faithfulness, righteousness and peace. The citation should include the verse material the card uses.
The card quotes verse 13 but also retells God's use of “Return” in verse 3, so Psalm 90:13 alone does not cite everything the card uses.
The card says that what the senseless man and fool do not understand is "about the wicked," but that detail comes from verse 7. The card cites only verse 6; it should cite Psalm 92:6-7.
Saying "There's that line again" relies on the earlier occurrence of "He is holy!" in verse 3, but the card cites only verse 5.
The contrast with worship at God's footstool retells verse 5, but the card's citation includes only verse 9.
The statement that the psalm calls God holy three times relies on verses 3, 5 and 9, while the card cites only verse 9.

The statement that God “outlasts the HEAVENS” uses verse 26's statement that the heavens will perish as well as verse 27's statement that God remains. Citing only verse 27 is too narrow; the card uses verses 26-27.

The card retells the lions withdrawing at sunrise from Psalm 104:22 in "The lions clock out," then tells about people going to work from Psalm 104:23. It cites only Psalm 104:23, so its citation should be Psalm 104:22-23.
The opening clause, 'He doesn't stop at looking,' uses verse 6, where the LORD humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth. Citing only verse 7 leaves out the earlier verse the card uses.

The phrase 'From the dump' uses verse 7, while the seat with nobles comes from verse 8 and the picture inside a home comes from verse 9. The citation begins at verse 8, so it does not cover everything the card uses.
The observation 'Same as the first' uses the Hallelujah in verse 1 as well as the closing Hallelujah in verse 9. Citing only verse 9 leaves out the earlier verse used by the card.
The card explicitly uses the dancing and tambourines from verse 3 as well as the reason introduced in verse 4, but it cites only Psalm 149:4. Its citation needs to begin with the first verse it uses.
The final sentence also tells that the book goes on to explain its purpose, drawing on the purpose statement in verses 2-6, but the card cites only verse 1.
The card tells Proverbs 5:23 but also recalls Proverbs 5:12 when it says the groaning son hated discipline. Its citation covers only verse 23, so it does not cite all the passage material it uses.

The card explicitly connects the wicked man sowing discord in Proverbs 6:14 with the last item in Proverbs 6:19, but it cites only Proverbs 6:19. Its citation needs to cover both verses used in the observation.
The card says the father then names two places to keep his teachings, which uses Proverbs 7:3, but it cites only Proverbs 7:2. The story card's citation should extend through verse 3.
The card retells Proverbs 22:17 when it says, "Back at the start it was ear and mind," but its citation includes only Proverbs 23:12.

The card uses Jeremiah 22:18 for "No mourning for Jehoiakim" and Jeremiah 22:19 for the donkey burial, but it cites only Jeremiah 22:19.
The opening sentence uses Jeremiah 22:25, including Coniah being handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, before telling Jeremiah 22:26. The citation therefore starts too late.
The opening sentence retells God's promise to bring the exiles home from Jeremiah 24:6, but the card cites only Jeremiah 24:9. Its citation does not cover everything the card tells.

The card explicitly tells the transition from the LORD's message about the whole land in verse 4 back to Baruch in verse 5, but it cites only verse 5. Under the exact-citation rule, its range should include both verses.

The phrase 'just a meal' tells a detail from the eating-and-drinking command in verse 18, but the card cites only verse 17. Its citation is narrower than the verses it uses.

The card retells Matthew 8:7 when it says Jesus is ready to head over, then introduces the centurion's answer in Matthew 8:8. Its story-card citation should therefore be Matthew 8:7-8, not only Matthew 8:8.

The card's observation that the girl repeats her mother's answer 'word for word' uses the mother's wording in Mark 6:24 as well as the girl's request in Mark 6:25. Citing only Mark 6:25 is too narrow; the card should cite Mark 6:24-25.
The opening sentence retells Mark 9:8 by saying that only Jesus is with Peter, James and John, but the card cites only Mark 9:9. Since the card also tells verse 9, its citation should be Mark 9:8-9.

The second sentence says these women knew Jesus earlier, back in the northern region where He started preaching. That relies on Mark 15:41, which says they had followed and ministered to Him in Galilee, but the card cites only Mark 15:40. Its citation is narrower than what the card tells.

The observation that Luke uses the same word for rebuking the fever and rebuking the demon relies on Luke 4:35 as well as Luke 4:39, but the card cites only Luke 4:39 and gives no reference for the earlier use.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

examples: The earlier cards have already established this answer: card 1 says the LORD attends to Sarah after promising a son, and card 3 says she bears the son right on God's schedule. This leaves nothing new for the baker to work out when asked whether the LORD did what He had promised.

The answer is given away before the question. Card 15 immediately says, 'God sent him ahead,' and card 12's question had already identified God as the one who sent Joseph to Egypt, so this choice merely repeats an answer the baker has already been given.

The question says Joseph's answer about raising livestock "will get them Goshen." This gives away the correct answer to card 7, which asks what the brothers request and whose right answer is "To let them settle in Goshen."

Card 8's right answer, "Their bodies and their land," already supplies this card's right answer, "Themselves and their land." This repeats the same answer rather than building on it with a new follow-up.

Calling Pharaoh's 600 best chariots "just the START" already indicates that more forces, including the other chariots, went with him. That gives away the False answer to card 8's statement that Pharaoh left every other chariot in Egypt.
This card says that the Israelites will see the LORD's glory "in the morning," directly supplying "morning" as the answer to the second blank on card 10 before that choice has been answered.

The answer 'veil' has already been given in card 10, which says that Moses puts a veil over his face, and is repeated in card 11's question. The blank is therefore answered before the baker reaches this card.

Card 11 already lists the sons' tunics, sashes and headbands, explicitly calls them "Three pieces each," and contrasts them with Aaron's much fuller outfit. It therefore gives away that the sons do not receive the exact same outfit before this question appears.
This card says that no one outside a priest's family may eat the sacred offering, directly settling card 14's question about the priest's guest and hired hand before that question is asked.
The line "A cloud in the sky" tells the baker that the cloud is still with Israel, giving away the answer "True" on card 16, which asks whether the cloud of the LORD is over them by day.

Stop 2 card 3 already says that God tells Moses to lay his hands on Joshua, and card 10 confirms that Moses does everything God commanded. This gives away the answer "Lays his hands on him" before card 12 asks what Moses does.

The answer is Pharaoh, but stop 1 card 16 already explicitly named "Pharaoh king of Egypt" without Pharaoh having been the answer to an earlier choice. That earlier story card gives away the answer to this later fill-in-the-blank question.

Card 16 has already said that there will always be "poor in the land" and that this is why Moses is giving the command. The correct answer then largely repeats that setup: "The poor and needy in their land."

Describing the crowd as "EVERYBODY" already establishes that the assembly is not limited to Israelite citizens. This gives away card 10, where the statement claiming that there are no foreigners is already known to be false.
By naming Jotham and summarizing his statement about fire consuming Shechem's leaders, this card hands the baker card 20's answer, "Jotham son of Jerubbaal," before asking whose curse came upon them.
Card 18 gives away the second blank's answer by saying 'Micah ordains the Levite' immediately before this choice asks for 'Levite.'

This card already says that Ahimaaz "won't let it go" and has him ask "no matter what" to run. That supplies the substance and key wording of card 6's correct answer, "He wants to run no matter what," before the question is asked.

Card 1 has already said that Barzillai came to cross the Jordan with the king and send him on his way. That gives away this card's conclusion that Barzillai will accompany David only a short distance past the Jordan rather than continuing with him.
Card 8 already says that Benaiah goes against the Egyptian with a club. That settles this later question about whether Benaiah backs away from the fight before the baker is asked it.
This card explicitly says that Solomon made Shimei swear by the LORD, supplying card 11's right answer, His oath to the LORD, before that choice is asked.
Card 13 has already said that Solomon does not know how to go out or come in. That directly gives away the answer to card 14, which asks whether Solomon says he already knows how to lead.
Card 7 has already named the supporting terraces, so it supplies the exact word needed for this later blank before the question appears.

Card 1 has already named Maacah daughter of Abishalom as Abijam's mother, and this card explicitly asks the baker to recall that name. The earlier story card therefore gives away the answer to this later choice card.

This story card explicitly says that Jehu strikes down everyone belonging to Ahab who remained in Samaria. Card 11 then asks the baker to affirm that same action, so the story card gives away the choice card's answer.

Saying that "not every man makes the count" already contradicts card 8's later statement that Joab finished counting all the men. The setup therefore gives away card 8's answer instead of letting it test verse 24's point that Joab did not finish.

The correct answer, that the people forsook the LORD for other gods, was already stated in card 13 and repeated in card 14's setup. Card 17 therefore asks for a cause that an earlier card has already given away.

Stop 1 card 11 has already stated plainly that Rehoboam rejected the elders' advice, and stop 1 cards 13-14 then supply the young men's harsher answer. Those cards already settle this card's claim that Rehoboam follows the elders and answers kindly, so the later choice is answered before it is asked.

Immediately after the rebuke about wrath, this card announces that Jehu is turning to 'the other side of the king's record.' That signals a positive statement and gives away the True answer to card 6, which asks whether some good is found in Jehoshaphat too.

Card 4 already says that they served Asherah poles and idols. Card 5 then asks what brought wrath, and its correct answer, "Their guilt in serving idols," merely restates what the baker was just told.
Stop 1, card 1 already says that Artaxerxes sent Ezra with silver and gold for God's house, essentially giving this card's correct answer verbatim before the question is asked.
Stop 1, card 1 already says that every Jew in the kingdom is to be destroyed. That gives away 'destroy' as the answer to this later fill-in-the-blank card.
Card 3 has already named Job's mouth, giving away the word needed for this blank before the baker chooses.
This card says that the enemies' tongues practice deceit, which already establishes that their words cannot be trusted and gives away the False answer to card 14.
By saying that God brings devastation "upon the earth," this card explicitly supplies "earth," the second correct answer on the following fill-in-the-blank card.
Card 5 has already told the baker that the man's heart is “withered like grass,” giving away “grass” as the answer to this later blank.

The opening card says that a man who lives many years should rejoice in them all. That directly supplies the key word in the correct answer to card 2, "Rejoice and let your heart be glad," before the baker is asked.

The story card says the invaders are coming 'to destroy the whole country,' immediately before card 9 asks what the Day of the LORD will come as, with 'destruction' as the answer. Saying 'destroy' hands the baker the answer rather than leaving the choice meaningful.
Story card 16 has just said that Israel "defiled the land," and this card's correct answer repeats that same statement, "Israel defiled the land." The preceding card therefore gives the answer away.
The final sentence explicitly says, "That's a Father talking about His kids," giving away "Father" as the correct answer to card 2's fill-in-the-blank question.

This story card identifies Israel as the kingdom the LORD called "faithless Israel." Together with Judah's already-established unfaithfulness in stop 1, that supplies the substance of card 5's True answer before the question is asked.
Card 7 explicitly says that the potter treats his clay, supplying the answer "clay" immediately before this card asks for it.
Card 16 has just mentioned "lightning flashing out of it." This immediately supplies the distinguishing word in card 17's correct answer, "As quick as flashes of lightning."

Stop 1 card 14 has already explained that two wings touch the wings of the creatures on either side. That earlier explanation supplies this card's answer, "Stretch out toward one another," rather than letting the new setup support a fresh choice.
Card 4 already says that nobody comes to take care of newborn Jerusalem. That rules out anyone washing her and wrapping her in cloths, giving away this card's answer before the baker chooses.

Card 8 has already said that the strong branches were stripped off, withered and consumed by fire. That establishes the answer to this card's claim that a strong branch still remains before the question is asked.

Stop 1 card 3 has already stated that Tyre's builders "perfected its beauty." Because this question explicitly says "Just like Tyre's builders," that earlier card supplies the blank's correct answer, "perfected."

Card 16 has already told the baker that God will make Seir desolate. Card 17 then says that Israel's inheritance became desolate and asks whether God will do the same, opposite, or a kinder thing to Seir, so the earlier card gives away the answer "same".

Card 1 already says that the LORD gave Haggai a message on the twenty-fourth day and now brings him another one, giving away this card's answer, True. The baker only has to repeat what the opening card stated.
This card says that the other side of the scroll goes after everyone who lies under oath, directly giving away card 6's correct answer, “The one who swears falsely by His name.”
Card 12 has already explicitly identified the cover as lead, so it gives away the second blank's correct answer, “lead,” before this choice.

The opening already identifies Joshua as the high priest. When card 6 later asks which named man is the high priest on whose head the crown is set, that earlier identification makes Joshua son of Jehozadak identifiable as the correct option before the question.

After the sea has become calm, this card explicitly says that Jesus asks the disciples why they are so afraid. That tells the baker their fear remains, giving away the False answer to card 16, which asks whether their fear is gone.

Card 10 already says that Jesus "starts listing" and includes adultery after murder, establishing before this question that the list does not stop at theft and murder. The baker can therefore mark the combined statement False without learning whether envy is included, which is the new detail this card purports to ask about.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

examples: The card adds the outside-passage fact that food had run low back home. Genesis 44:23-25 does not state that detail; it comes from the preceding context in Genesis 43:1-2, so it needs its own reference.

Genesis 50:24 does not name the promised land as Canaan. That identification depends on other Genesis passages, but no reference to those passages is supplied, so the correct answer is not supported by the citation or an outside reference.

Aaron being Moses's brother is an identifying fact from outside Exodus 9:13-35. The card's citation, Exodus 9:27, names Aaron but does not state that relationship, and no supporting reference is supplied for it.

The identification of Solomon as king of Israel is not stated in 1 Kings 9:1. This outside Bible fact needs its own supporting reference, as the Gibeon detail receives on card 3.

Jehu's role as commander, his recent anointing, and the commanders' proclamation come from 2 Kings 9:5-13, but no reference is supplied for them. The card's citation of 2 Kings 9:14-15 does not cover those facts.
The description of Judah as one of Jacob's sons is a fact from outside 1 Chronicles 4:1–8, but no reference supporting that relationship is given.
Calling Simeon Judah's brother adds a relationship not stated in 1 Chronicles 4:24–37, and the card gives no reference for that outside fact.
Calling Judah "another son of Israel" adds a relationship that verse 2 does not state, but no supporting reference is given for that outside fact.
Calling Saul "King Saul" adds his kingship, which verse 10 does not state, without giving a reference for that outside identification.

The temple's completion is previous-passage context, not something stated in Ezra 7:1-6. The card uses that outside fact without giving its reference, so the citation does not cover everything the card tells.

The description of Ezra as "a priest and scribe" is a Bible fact from outside Ezra 9:1-15, but it has no supporting reference. The card's Ezra 9:1 citation and its parenthetical Ezra 8:32-35 reference do not establish that role.

The card identifies the king as "King Xerxes of Persia," but its citation to Esther 9:1 supports only "the king." Xerxes is named in the next verse, and the added identification as Persia's king has no supporting reference.

Calling David "king of Israel" uses a fact that Psalm 6:1 does not state. The card gives no supporting reference for that outside-passage detail; it needs one, or David can be introduced without the title.
Calling David "son of Jesse" adds a fact that is not in Psalm 21:1. The card cites only Psalm 21:1, so this outside identification has no supporting reference.

The card adds the outside-passage fact that David was Israel's king, but its only reference is Psalm 27:1, which does not state that fact. The outside fact needs its own reference.
The card adds the outside-passage fact that David was Israel's king, but Psalm 40:1 does not state that, and no supporting reference is given for it.
The card identifies Saul as king of Israel, but Psalm 54:1 only names Saul. This supporting fact from outside the passage is given no reference of its own.

Calling David 'king of Israel' uses a fact from outside Psalm 58, but no reference supporting that fact is provided. Psalm 58:1 identifies David and the tune, not his kingship.

Calling David 'king of Israel' adds a fact that Psalm 65:1 does not state. The card's only citation covers the psalm's superscription and opening verse, so this helpful outside identification lacks its own supporting reference.
David is identified as "Israel's king," but Psalm 86:1 does not state that fact, and no reference is supplied for it. This outside Bible fact needs its own reference.
The card adds the outside-passage facts that David was a shepherd and became king of Israel, but Psalm 103:1 supports neither fact and no other reference is given for them.
The question uses the outside Bible fact that God renamed Jacob as Israel, but gives no reference for that renaming. The card's citation of Psalm 114:1 does not support it.

Calling David "king of Israel" is a Bible fact from outside Psalm 139. The card cites only Psalm 139:1, which identifies this as a psalm of David but does not support his kingship, so the outside fact lacks its own reference.

The description of Solomon as son of David and king of Israel comes from Proverbs 1:1, outside this passage, but the card gives no reference for that fact and cites only Proverbs 8:1.

The outside-passage reference does not support the whole identification of Solomon. Proverbs 10:1 identifies these sayings as Solomon's proverbs, but it does not call him king of Israel; Proverbs 1:1 supplies that identification.

The card adds that Pharaoh is Egypt's king, but that identification is not stated in this passage and no reference is given for it. Solomon's comparable identification on card 1 does carry a reference.
The identifications of Jacob as Israel's forefather and Judah as the tribe of Jacob's son Judah are facts outside Isaiah 65:9, but neither identification carries its own reference.
The opening adds the outside fact that Jeremiah is a prophet, but the cited Jeremiah 2:20 neither names Jeremiah nor establishes that role, and no supporting reference is given.

The description of Judah as "the kingdom of His people in the south" is outside Jeremiah 2:28. That background fact needs its own supporting reference rather than only the citation for Judah's many gods.

The card adds the outside-passage facts that Moses was Israel's leader and Samuel was a prophet, but gives no references for those identifications. Jeremiah 15:1 names both men but does not establish either role.
The description of Daniel as a man of Judah carried off to Babylon is background from Daniel 1, not Daniel 9:1-2. It is useful background, but no reference accompanies that outside fact.
The card adds the outside Bible fact that David was Israel's king but gives no reference for that identification. Amos 6:5 supplies the comparison to David, not his position as king.
Calling Joseph "Mary's husband" uses a fact not stated in Matthew 2:13-23, but no supporting reference is supplied for that identification. Matthew 2:13 does not state his relationship to Mary.
The card introduces Jesus as "God's Son," but Matthew 21:1 does not state that. This outside Bible fact is given without a supporting reference.

The description of the Pharisees as "a Jewish group known for strictly keeping the Law" is background from outside the passage, but no reference supports it. Matthew 21:45 names the Pharisees without supplying that description.

The detail that Mary Magdalene was one of the women who followed Jesus from Galilee comes from Matthew 27:55-56, not Matthew 28:1. The card cites only Matthew 28:1, so this outside fact does not carry its supporting reference.

The card adds facts not stated in Mark 12:35: Jesus is God's Son, the scribes are teachers of the law, and the Christ is God's promised King. Those outside-passage facts are given without their references.
Calling David Israel's king uses an outside-passage fact, but the card gives no reference for it; Mark 12:36 does not identify David as king.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what.

examples: The question never identifies the boy as Ishmael or connects him to Hagar. The boy and he depend on cards that are no longer visible rather than giving the needed context within the question itself.

"What else" points back to the tree planting on the previous story card, which is no longer visible, without identifying that action. The question should supply its own context, such as mentioning that Abraham has planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba.

The question relies on the previous story card for the antecedent of "them." On its own, it never identifies the people Pharaoh is refusing to let go; name them as the LORD's people or the Israelites in the question.

"After all of this" points back to the ceremony on earlier cards. The question does not identify what has been completed, so it is not self-contained when the preceding story card is no longer visible.

"All of these inheritances" points back to the preceding story card without identifying the tribal inheritances or their distribution, so the question does not supply its own context.

On its own, "Inside each man's large jar" does not identify whose men or jars these are. The question depends on the preceding story card to supply that these are the jars Gideon gave his three hundred men.

The word "instead" depends on the previous cards for its antecedent: Elisha's rejection of killing the Arameans. The question should supply that context itself rather than requiring the baker to remember a card that is no longer on screen.

The question asks the baker to add David's two reigns but omits both figures, seven years and six months and thirty-three years. Those necessary details appear only on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen.
The opening “they” has no antecedent on the choice card. The baker must remember the previous story card to know that it means the gatekeepers put in charge of the worship articles.
“Their Kohathite relatives” depends on earlier cards to establish whose relatives these are. The question needs to identify the antecedent within its own wording.
The question depends on 'this group' without identifying the group as the Benjamites and men from Judah. Once the earlier story card is gone, the question does not supply that context itself.
The question depends on 'these men' without identifying them as the armed men who came to David at Hebron, so it relies on context from a card the baker can no longer see.

The phrase 'those nations' depends on the preceding story card for its meaning. The choice card itself never identifies the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, so it lacks the necessary context when shown on its own.
The question begins, "They gather their brothers," without identifying them as the Levites. That identification depends on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen.

The question begins, "They bring bulls, rams, lambs and male goats," without identifying who "They" are. It points back to Hezekiah and the city officials on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen.
The question depends on "all those treasures," but the treasures are identified only on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to identify the treasures itself.

Several choice cards rely on referents from cards that are no longer on screen: card 2 says these young men, card 4 says they, card 5 says these men and card 11 says that mud. The questions should restate enough context, such as identifying the younger men who mock Job and saying that God has thrown Job into the mud.

The question does not identify what "these things" and "them" are. Without the earlier cards, the baker cannot tell what warns God's servant or what David says should be kept. Name the LORD's Law, testimonies, precepts, commandments, and judgments, or summarize them with a clear term such as God's words.

"What does Ethan ask the LORD?" is a bare prompt once the preceding story card is gone. It needs the immediate context of the king's ruin and shame so the baker can understand the moment and reason toward Ethan's cry.
The question begins "He ends this stretch" without identifying "He" as the psalmist. It relies on earlier cards for its context instead of saying who is acting within the question itself.

The question begins with "He calls to the LORD" without identifying who "He" is. With the opening story card no longer on screen, the pronoun depends on context the baker cannot see; the question should identify the writer.

The question's "this" points back to the previous card without saying what must not wait. Once that card is gone, the question does not explain that Solomon is telling the son to get free from his pledge by going to his neighbor.

The question depends on 'those cities,' but their only antecedent is on story card 12, which is no longer on screen. The choice card never identifies them as the fortified cities crushed into rubble, so it does not provide its own context.
The question uses "His" without identifying whose clothes are being discussed. It depends on earlier cards instead of giving the baker self-contained context.
The question uses "He" and "His" without identifying the speaker, so it does not stand on its own after the preceding story card leaves the screen.
The question does not identify who "He" is. Mentioning the day of vengeance supplies the topic but not the needed context for the speaker.
The question never identifies who "He" is, leaving its subject dependent on cards the baker can no longer see.

The question depends on "the picture of the race" from card 10, but that story card is no longer on screen and the question does not restate the race. The question itself needs the comparison between racing men on foot and competing with horses.
"These same people" depends on the preceding story card for its meaning. The question should identify them as Jeremiah's accusers or the people plotting against him.
With the setup card no longer on screen, "for them" does not identify whose disobedience is being discussed. The question needs its own context, such as the people who refused the LORD's warning.
The question never identifies who 'them' and 'their' refer to. It depends on the preceding card's mention of Israel and Judah instead of giving that context in the question itself.
The question never names the people whose cause and lovers are being discussed. Both uses of 'their' rely on earlier cards rather than identifying the LORD's people in the question.
The question does not say whose wound, health and wounds these are. 'Their' points back to earlier cards instead of identifying Zion or the LORD's people on this card.
The word 'them' has no antecedent on the card. The callback to the cry of panic does not identify Israel and Judah or the LORD's people as the ones from whom thanksgiving will come.
The phrase 'their leader and ruler' has no antecedent on the card. The question relies on earlier cards to identify whose leader is being discussed.
The question does not identify whose case the LORD is pleading. “Their” points back to Israel and Judah, who are named only on earlier cards, rather than giving that context in the question itself.

The question's 'they' has no antecedent on the choice card. Only the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen, identifies the people as Israel and their kings. The question needs to name them itself.

"Their" and "them" have no antecedent within the question, so identifying the people requires remembering earlier cards that are no longer visible. Name the people being addressed in the question itself.
The question's 'They'll' has no antecedent on the choice card. With the preceding story card no longer visible, the question does not identify whom Nahum is describing.

The question relies on card 18 for the contrast behind "But" and "actually": the deceiver has an acceptable male and vows to give it. Since that story card is no longer on screen, the question needs to restate that setup.
The question begins with “They” but never identifies who they are. That antecedent appears only on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen.

The question does not identify whose faith Jesus sees. “Their” has no plural antecedent within the question, since only the man on the mat and Jesus are mentioned, so it relies on an earlier card for context.

The wrong answer "They agree to march in" is arguable later in the passage. In Numbers 14:40, the people say they will go to the place the LORD promised and set out toward the hill country, so this answer is not clearly false anywhere in the passage.

The wrong answer "He may flee to a city of refuge" uses something that is true elsewhere in this passage for the unintentional manslayer, notably in verses 11, 15 and 25, rather than being false anywhere in the passage.

The wrong answers 'While protecting his own family' and 'In a fight his neighbor started' do not necessarily exclude an unintentional killing without prior malice. Either circumstance could still satisfy verse 42, so a baker could argue that either answer fits.

The wrong answer "The elders of each tribe" is arguably true. The elders are explicitly among those standing before the LORD in Deuteronomy 29:10, so they are included in the "us" to whom the revealed things belong in Deuteronomy 29:29. It gives a subset of the correct answer rather than a clearly false alternative.

The distractor "Stand and fight them" is not false throughout the passage: Joshua and all Israel later turn around and strike down the men of Ai (Joshua 8:21). Use a distractor that never happens in Joshua 8:1-29.
The wrong answer "Ask for another sign with the fleece" is not false everywhere in the passage. Gideon does exactly that in Judges 6:39, making the distractor true at an earlier moment.

The wrong answer "Every single survivor ends up with a wife" is not false throughout the passage. Although the 400 women are not enough in verse 14, the Benjamites later take "the number of women they needed" from the dancers in verse 23, so this option can describe the final outcome.

The wrong answer "Move it to the next Philistine city" is not false anywhere in the passage. Moving the ark to another Philistine city is exactly what happens when it goes to Gath and then Ekron in verses 8-10.

The wrong answer "They finally have a king to lead them" is true elsewhere in the passage: Samuel says the LORD has placed the king they requested over them (1 Samuel 12:13). It is not the reason given in verse 22, but the distractor itself is not false anywhere in the passage.

The wrong answer "Take the best of it as plunder" is not false throughout the passage. Saul and his troops later spare the best animals, and Saul says the troops took the best of the plunder (1 Samuel 15:9, 21).

The wrong answers are not reliably false. Jonathan strengthens David and makes a covenant with him later in this passage, so a baker could reasonably argue that Jonathan also would not deliver David into Saul's hand. Abiathar is likewise presented as David's ally, not as someone who would betray him.

The intended wrong answer, True, is not false everywhere in the passage. David is unwilling to move the ark in 2 Samuel 6:10, but after asking the question in verse 9 he does later have it brought into the City of David in verse 12. Because the statement says only 'After asking' rather than 'right then,' a baker could reasonably argue that True is correct.
The wrong answer "Stand there without a word" is true earlier in the passage: the people did not answer Elijah a word in 1 Kings 18:21. It is false only at this later moment.
The wrong answer “He went to see Naaman” describes something that actually happens in 2 Kings 5:21-22. It is not Gehazi's reply in verse 25, but it is still true elsewhere in the passage.
The wrong answer "mourning" is not false throughout the passage. Nehemiah 8:9 describes the people weeping and tells them not to mourn; it is false only at the moment described in Nehemiah 8:17.

The wrong answer 'Maybe Haman has a plan against her too' is not safely false. Haman's decree targets all the Jews, and Mordecai has just warned Esther that she will not escape their fate, so a baker could reasonably regard this option as true.

The wrong answer A hard life surrounded by enemies is not false everywhere in the passage. In Job 30:12-14, Job describes the rabble laying snares, building siege ramps and advancing against him, so this option resembles his present suffering even though it was not what he expected in Job 29:18.

The wrong answer “How hard each one works” is something Solomon compares elsewhere in this passage: Proverbs 10:4 contrasts idle hands with diligent hands. It is therefore not false anywhere in the passage.
Loving "when things go well" and "when love is returned" are both included in loving "at all times." A baker could defend either alternative, so neither is a reliably false answer.

The distractor "A fresh start once they turn back" is arguably true elsewhere in the passage: verses 3-7 offer a way back if the people correct their ways, and card 4 itself calls this "a way back." Use a distractor that is not true elsewhere in the passage.
"warned" is not unambiguously false in the passage. Jeremiah 23:21 also says that the LORD did not speak to these prophets, so a baker could reasonably understand that He never warned them.

The wrong answer "Ebed-melech stepped in to defend him" describes something that really happened earlier in this passage, in Jeremiah 38:7-10. It is not why the officials stop questioning Jeremiah in verse 27, but a wrong answer cannot simply be true at a different moment in the passage.

The wrong answer "That Gog has fallen" is true in Ezekiel 39:4-5. Although it is not what verse 6 says Magog and the coastlands will know, the distractor itself is not false everywhere in the passage.

The wrong answer 'The covenant with all the nations' describes something that actually happens in this passage: verse 10 says cutting the staff called Favor revoked that covenant. It is therefore not false everywhere in the passage.

The wrong answer "You have kept the matter quiet" is arguably true: the confrontation was private, and when the brother listens, Jesus gives no instruction to tell anyone else. A baker could reasonably defend this answer.

rule.text: For who, which thing and where questions, wrong answers are real details from somewhere in the Bible, like Joppa when the right answer is Tarshish.

examples: This is a where question, but the wrong answers "Around the edge of Abram's camp" and "Up into the darkened sky" are invented locations rather than real details from somewhere in the Bible.
This is a where question, but neither wrong answer is a real detail from elsewhere in the Bible. Scripture does not mention Joseph having a house in Goshen or a temple at On.

This is a where question, but its distractors are invented locations rather than real details from somewhere in the Bible. In particular, the Bible does not describe putting this blood on an altar outside the camp or on the horns of cattle; it is an altar, not cattle, whose horns receive blood in other passages.

This is a where question, but the wrong answer "In his house in town" invents a location for Boaz rather than using a real detail from somewhere in the Bible.

This is a where question, but the wrong answer "The houses of the city's elders" is an invented location rather than a real detail from somewhere in the Bible.

This is a which-things question, but the wrong answer "The old stones from the repair work" is invented. The temple-repair account mentions buying timber and dressed stone, not old stones (2 Kings 22:6).

This is a where question, but its wrong answers are generic fundraising methods rather than real details from elsewhere in the Bible. In particular, "Selling off the royal farmland" is an invented action, not a biblical detail used as a distractor.
This is a where question, but the wrong answer "Through the shield on his arm" is an invented wound detail, not a real detail from somewhere in the Bible.

This is a where question, but the wrong answer "To a quiet house in Babylon" is invented rather than being a real detail from somewhere in the Bible. Babylon is biblical, but a quiet house there is not.

The wrong answer "Only the language of Susa" invents a language rather than using a real language detail from somewhere in the Bible. This is a which-language question, so its wrong answers need to be real Bible details.
This is a who question, but the wrong answer "Job's neighbors in Uz" is not a real detail from somewhere in the Bible. Job's neighbors in Uz are never mentioned.

This is a who question, but the wrong answers are invented categories rather than real details from somewhere in the Bible. In particular, people waiting too long and people asking too many questions are not biblical details being reused as distractors.
This is a who question, but the distractor "A mighty warrior at the gate" is an invented description rather than an identifiable detail from elsewhere in the Bible.
This is a who question, but the wrong answer "Ourselves" is a generic invented alternative rather than a real detail from somewhere in the Bible.

This is a who question, but the wrong answer 'Those who never stumble at all' is not a real detail from somewhere in the Bible; James 3:2 says that we all stumble in many ways. The other wrong answer, those who serve in the temple, is a real biblical detail.
This is a who question, but "Those who build behind high walls" is a generic invented alternative rather than an identifiable real detail from somewhere in the Bible.

This is a who question, but the wrong answer about kings carrying Zion's sons is not a real Bible detail. It combines the nations carrying her children in Isaiah 49:22 with the kings in Isaiah 49:23, rather than using a real detail as the distractor.
This is a "which animal" question, but "A dove caught in a net" is not a real detail from somewhere in the Bible. The wrong answers to this kind of question must be real Bible details.

For this which-thing question, the distractor 'His vineyard in Bethlehem' is an invented property-and-location pairing rather than a real detail from somewhere in the Bible. Bethlehem appears in Scripture, but a vineyard in Bethlehem is not an identifiable biblical detail.

This is a who question, but the distractor "Babylon's priests" is not an identifiable group or detail from somewhere in the Bible. It reads as an invented plausible answer rather than the real biblical detail required for this kind of question.

This is a where question about the calf's origin, but the wrong answers invent origin stories for the calf. Being carried in from Egypt and being a gift from Assyria are not real details from somewhere else in the Bible.
This is a where question, but "In a city by the sea" is a generic invented location rather than a real detail from somewhere in the Bible.
This is a where question, but the wrong answer 'Half south and half west' is an invented direction pair rather than a real detail from somewhere in the Bible.

rule.text: A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

examples: Most of this stop's choices require luck rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. The setup withholds any basis for reasoning out the number of men (card 2), Rachel's placement (card 4), the number of bows (card 6), Esau's response (card 7), Jacob's description of the children (card 9), and the two gift outcomes (cards 12 and 17). These seven discovery questions make up most of the stop's nine choices, rather than being the allowed few.

Discovery questions dominate the walkthrough rather than remaining a few exceptions. For example, the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (stop 1, card 5), atonement (card 7), Aaron's sons (card 9), the north side of the altar (card 16), the permitted birds (card 18), or not dividing the bird completely (card 20). Stops 2 and 3 similarly leave most ingredients, portions and durations to be guessed rather than reasoned from what has already been told.

Too much of stop 1 depends on discovery guesses rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Cards 2, 4, 6, 9 and 14 ask for Mount Seir, the direction north, the fear of Esau's descendants, God's reason for withholding their land and the next road without giving the baker a basis to infer those answers. That is five of the stop's eight choices, so this stop becomes more of a guessing game than the allowed occasional discovery question.

Stop 1 card 2 gives no basis for the tribes' description of themselves, card 8 no basis for David's age, and card 10 no basis for the city; stop 2 card 2 gives no hint of the blind-and-lame taunt, card 4 no basis for Zion, card 6 no hint of the water shaft, and card 8 no basis for the extent of the building. Too many choices require discovering an unrevealed detail rather than reasoning from the setup. Cards 2, 5, 9, 13 and 15 give no contextual basis for eliminating the alternatives: the meeting-place problem, the extra request made to Elisha, why losing the axe head is worse, what Elisha cuts, and who retrieves the axe head. That makes five of the nine choice cards discoveries rather than informed guesses.

Discovery questions are too frequent for reasoned choices to be the norm. The earlier cards give no basis for identifying Joram's visitor (stop 1, card 4), choosing what Joram shouts for (stop 1, card 13), deciding whether Joram's body should be thrown, buried, or burned (stop 1, card 18), predicting Jezebel's response to Jehu's arrival (stop 2, card 6), or knowing what Jehu does after going inside (stop 2, card 11). Several other true-or-false and fill-in-the-blank cards likewise introduce facts or wording the baker cannot infer.

Four of the six choice cards depend on luck or prior Bible knowledge rather than the earlier cards: card 2 asks for the officer's name, card 4 for Pekah's exact reign length, card 6 for the captured people's fate, and card 10 for the gate's name. Only the conspiracy pattern in card 7 and the LORD's activity in card 11 offer a reasonable basis for an informed pick, so most choices in this stop are not informed guesses.

Most of this stop's choices are not informed guesses. Cards 2, 4, 7, 11 and 15 ask for Josiah's exact age, whether he follows Amon, what Hilkiah is to count, whether the workers must account for the money, and which report Shaphan gives first without earlier cards supplying a basis for reasoning out the answers. At least five of the nine choices therefore depend on luck, rather than only a few discovery questions among mostly informed picks.

Cards 2, 3, 5, 9, 14 and 16 ask the baker to discover wording or an outcome that the earlier cards give no sufficient basis to reason out. Six of the nine choice cards are therefore discoveries, so most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses.

Five of the ten choice cards (4, 6, 8, 9 and 13) depend on unrevealed details that cannot be inferred from the earlier cards: what Ahaz makes, the other worship sites, Damascus, Israel and Samaria. Half the stop therefore relies on discovery guesses rather than using them as a few exceptions among mostly informed choices.

Cards 3, 4, 8 and 14 offer plausible alternatives without setup that distinguishes the right answer, and card 9 asks for an unseen word. Only cards 7, 11 and 12 clearly provide a basis for reasoning, so most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses.

Together with the ambiguous blank on card 11, these go beyond a few discovery questions and leave reasoned choices in the minority.

A baker who does not already know the passage has to guess.

For example, the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out the attackers' direction (stop 1, card 4), what the LORD says about Israel and Judah (stop 1, card 8), where to tell the news (stop 1, card 18), which kings are stirred up (stop 2, card 2), what the LORD swears by (stop 2, card 7), or the content of the locust oath (stop 2, card 8). The setups commonly withhold a fact and immediately ask for it.

Discovery questions dominate the stop. Cards 2, 3, 7, 9, 15, 17 and 19 ask for unseen numbers, imagery or wording without earlier-card context that supports a reasoned pick, so most of the ten choices depend on luck rather than informed guesses.

This stop becomes a guessing game. Cards 2, 6, 7, 9 and 16, five of its nine choice cards, give no prior basis for reasoning out the covenant, the optional wages, the potter, the location, or the sword's target. That is more than a few discovery questions within the stop.

Most of the choices are not informed guesses. Cards 4, 5, 9, 13, 15 and 17 ask for facts for which the earlier cards provide no clue, leaving a baker who has seen only those cards to rely on luck or prior knowledge. Discovery questions therefore make up six of the nine choices rather than just a few.

This stop relies too heavily on discovery questions. Cards 2, 4, 6, 16 and 18 ask for facts that cannot be inferred from the earlier cards: whether to enter Samaritan towns, whether to raise the dead, how the twelve received, how to respond to rejection and which two cities Jesus names. A baker who does not already know the passage must guess rather than reason through most of the stop's choices.

Too many choices depend on luck or prior Bible knowledge rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Card 3 asks for locations not yet revealed, card 10 for Jesus' unrevealed response, card 14 for mission details not yet explained, and cards 16, 17 and 19 for an arbitrary new name, an untranslated name and an unrevealed betrayal. Together with the unsupported 50/50 statement in card 2, these go beyond a few discovery questions.

Too many choices rely on discovery rather than informed reasoning. Cards 2, 3, 9, 11, 12 and 14 provide no basis in the earlier cards for reasoning out their answers. That is at least six of the eleven choice cards, so most choices are not informed guesses.

Cards 2, 3, 5, 8 and 11 all ask for details that the earlier cards neither supply nor make inferable: praying rather than teaching, the Holy Spirit, the dove, "My beloved Son" and Jesus' age. Nearly every choice is therefore discovery or luck rather than an informed guess.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer. The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question. A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

examples: Cards 2, 6, 8, 10, 11, 14 and 18 ask for details that earlier cards neither supply nor make inferable: Sarah's exact age, the Hittites' exact offer, full price, Ephron's gift, whether the field is included, silver and the trees. Seven of the ten choices therefore depend on discovery or luck, so most of the stop's choice cards are not informed guesses.

Stop 1 relies on luck repeatedly rather than using only a few discovery questions. Cards 2, 3, 4, 7, 9, 13, 15 and 18 ask for facts that cannot be inferred from the earlier cards. For example, an altar before the calf gives no basis for knowing that Aaron proclaims the feast to the LORD, and nothing before cards 15 and 18 supplies "nation" or the patriarchs' names.

The mirror question could serve as one discovery question, but with the horn and two tribal-affiliation questions, most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses.

Only a few discovery questions are allowed; most choice cards need setups or replacement questions that let the baker reason from what has already been told.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

examples: Neither the setup nor any earlier card gives Joseph's birth order or says that he was born to Israel in his old age. A baker using only the earlier cards can only guess whether the firstborn statement is true, and the actual reason Genesis 37:3 gives for Israel's love is never supplied elsewhere.

Card 14 says only that Israel rebuked Joseph. It gives no basis for deciding whether Israel then dismissed the dream or kept it in mind, so the baker must guess. The true action in Genesis 37:11, Israel keeping Joseph's words in mind, is not told on any card.

This choice reduces Genesis 47:28 to guessing two unheard numbers. Nothing in the earlier cards gives the baker any basis for either seventeen years or 147 years, so someone who does not already know the verse can only make a 50/50 guess.

The baker therefore cannot reason out whether God's people hand their riches to the nations. The actual promise that they will feed on the wealth of nations and boast in their riches is not told afterward either.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

The setup says only that the five kings were brought out of the cave. Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason whether Joshua commands the commanders to put their feet on the kings' necks, heads, or backs.
The setup says only that Israel besieged Lachish and fought against it. It gives no basis for choosing the second day rather than the third or seventh, making this blank a guess at an unseen detail.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

examples: The blank lets the baker eliminate both wrong answers grammatically: only LORD agrees with hardens, while the magicians hardens and the officials hardens do not. The right answer therefore stands out without the baker needing to understand Exodus 9:12.
The article "an" makes only "enemy" grammatical in the blank; "friend" and "stranger" would require "a." The wording therefore makes the correct answer stand out.
The correct answer stands out through its biblical wording, "defile" and "dwells," while both wrong answers use modern, everyday wording about resting, healing and catching something.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

examples: The wrong answer "still" is also defensible: God's work had already been called good, and the completed creation remains good. A baker could argue for it, leaving the card to hinge on the exact unseen adverb rather than a clearly false alternative.

Both wrong answers name people who are also supposed to attend. Every man from each tribe is included in the command to assemble the men, and the priests and elders are part of Israel. Since neither option says "only," a baker could reasonably argue that either answer is true; they are incomplete rather than clearly false.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.
